security-mindset-risk.text: A user changes one number in a URL — /orders/1043 becomes /orders/1044 — and reads a stranger's invoice. No password cracked, no exploit kit: the endpoint authenticated the user and then simply forgot to ask whether this user owns this object. That single missing check is OWASP's #1 web risk, and it ships in production every day.

Security is not a feature you bolt on; it is a mindset you apply to every boundary an action crosses. This lesson turns 'be careful' into a reviewable artifact — assets, trust boundaries, least-privilege controls, and evidence — the packet you will reuse in the course capstone.

security-mindset-risk.prompt: An endpoint checks 'is this request logged in?' before returning an order. Is that request now secure? Answer before reading on.
security-mindset-risk.reveal: No — it proved identity (authentication) but never checked entitlement (authorization). Knowing WHO you are is not permission to see THIS object. The endpoint authenticated the user and then trusted the object id from the URL, so any logged-in user can read any order by incrementing the id. This is a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR) flaw — OWASP API #1 — and it feels secure precisely because the login worked.

security-mindset-risk.title: Security mindset: name the asset, draw the trust boundary, enforce least privilege, prove denial
security-mindset-risk.text: For every action, ask: what asset is exposed, where does it cross a trust boundary, what is the least privilege that permits it, and what abuse defeats a weak control? The invariant: authorization is checked at the boundary, per-object, and the denial is proven — not assumed.

security-mindset-risk.title: Where the trust boundary lives — and where it is forgotten
security-mindset-risk.subtitle: A GET /orders/:id request. Authentication answers 'who'; the object-level authorization check answers 'may this who touch THIS object'. The failure path (no ownership check) leaks the asset; the repair path (check owner_id) denies it.

the trust boundary — per-object authorization

security-mindset-risk.title: Building the least-privilege control — the artifact from the packet
security-mindset-risk.subtitle: The weak handler trusts the URL id; the gold handler scopes the query to the caller and proves the deny. This block is section 'Selected approach' of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md.
security-mindset-risk.code:
# WEAK — authenticated, but no object-level authorization
def get_order_weak(request, order_id):
    user = require_auth(request)          # proves WHO — that's all it proves
    order = db.orders.find(id=order_id)   # trusts the id from the URL
    return order                          # BOLA: any user reads any order

# GOLD — least privilege enforced AT the trust boundary
def get_order(request, order_id):
    user = require_auth(request)
    order = db.orders.find(id=order_id, owner_id=user.id)  # scope to caller
    if order is None:
        audit.log('order.read.deny', user=user.id, target=order_id)
        raise Forbidden(403)              # prove the denial, don't leak existence
    audit.log('order.read.allow', user=user.id, target=order_id)
    return order

steps.label: Authentication is not authorization
steps.note: require_auth proves the caller is a valid user. That is necessary and NOT sufficient — it says nothing about this object.

steps.label: The BOLA flaw
steps.note: The weak version looks up the order by the id from the URL. Increment the id, read a stranger's order. This is the exact mechanism behind OWASP API #1.

steps.label: Least privilege at the boundary
steps.note: The gold version scopes the query with owner_id=user.id. The database can only return an object the caller owns — the authorization check is the query itself, per-object.

steps.label: Prove the denial, hide existence
steps.note: On a non-owned id the row is None → return 403, and log it. Returning 403 (not 404-with-details) avoids leaking whether the object exists.

steps.label: Audit evidence for both outcomes
steps.note: Log the allow AND the deny. The audit log is the evidence a reviewer inspects — 'order.read.deny' is the line that proves the control fired.

security-mindset-risk.caption: Proof: curl the endpoint as user B for user A's order id → HTTP 403 + one 'order.read.deny' audit line. That denied request IS the artifact.

security-mindset-risk.text: OWASP grounding: Broken Object Level Authorization is API Security Top 10 #1 (2023) and the engine behind classic IDOR in Web Top 10 A01 Broken Access Control. The reason it dominates real breaches is that authentication is easy to see working — the login succeeds — while the missing per-object check is invisible until an attacker (or a curious user) increments an id. The mindset move is to treat every object id from the client as attacker-controlled input until the boundary proves ownership.

security-mindset-risk.question: Reviewer challenge: which single piece of evidence best proves your access control actually works — not just that the happy path runs?
options: A screenshot of the legitimate owner successfully loading their own order (HTTP 200).
A failing unauthorized request — user B asking for user A's order id returns 403 — with a matching 'deny' line in the audit log.
A comment in the code that says '# authorization enforced here'.
The fact that every user must log in before reaching the endpoint.
security-mindset-risk.explanation: The security claim lives in the DENIED request. A 200 for the owner (1) exercises the happy path and says nothing about an attacker. A comment (3) is not enforcement, and login (4) is authentication, not authorization. Only the proven 403 + the matching audit-log 'deny' line shows the object-level control actually fired against an abuse case — that is the reusable evidence.

security-mindset-risk.intro: Prove your packet holds — no vibes:
items: Name the asset in one line (what data/action is exposed) and mark exactly where it crosses a trust boundary. If you cannot point to the boundary, you have not modeled the threat.
Show the control is per-object, not just per-role: the check must reference THIS object's owner, not merely 'is an admin/user'.
Run the abuse case: as a different user, request an object you do not own. Capture the actual 403/denied response — not a description of one.
Find the matching 'deny' line in the audit log. If the denial is not logged, you have no evidence it fired.
State the rejected control and why it loses (e.g. role-only check misses object-level ownership), and write one reviewer objection you would have to answer.

Walk your packet's trust boundary out loud: what asset crosses it, what least-privilege control guards it, and what abuse case would defeat a weaker version.
Point to the exact evidence in your packet that proves the control is not just a happy-path answer — the denied request and its audit line — and say why a comment or a login gate would not count.

security-mindset-risk.text: The same mindset — asset, trust boundary, least privilege, proven denial — transfers to every boundary in the course. Multi-tenant SaaS: the boundary is the tenant_id, the abuse case is one tenant reading another's rows, the control is row-level scoping, the evidence is a cross-tenant 403. Cloud IAM: the asset is an S3 object, the boundary is the policy, least privilege replaces 's3:*' with a scoped action, and the proof is a denied AccessDenied in CloudTrail. What stays invariant is the packet; what changes is the asset and the attacker path. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the security capstone — it is reused directly as the threat model + access-control evidence behind the exploit regression, IAM policy, and incident runbook.

identity-authentication.proof: Section 1 ("Identity & Authentication Boundary") of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: named identity assets, the trust boundary drawn explicitly, the authentication invariant stated as a testable claim, and one concrete abuse case that would break it. A reviewer can point to the exact line the invariant lives on and name a request that should be rejected.
identity-authentication.unlock: Your Section 1 names the identity assets, draws the trust boundary a credential crosses, and states a single falsifiable authentication invariant with one abuse case against it.
identity-authentication.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have "handled authentication" because you have a login form and a password check. Authentication is a proven invariant at a trust boundary, not a feature that exists. If you cannot write the exact unauthorized request that must be rejected and show it IS rejected, you have a login page, not a control.

identity-authentication.text: The pentester does not guess passwords. She replays a session token from a logged-out user, and the API answers as if the session were still alive — because someone shipped authentication as a login screen and never proved the invariant behind it. One reused token, one crossed boundary, and "who are you" quietly became "whoever holds this string."

Authentication is the first control in Security & Identity Engineering: it decides who a request is before authorization decides what they may do. Get this boundary wrong and every downstream control — least privilege, object access, audit — is guarding a door whose lock never actually latched.

identity-authentication.prompt: "Users log in with email and password, and we hash the passwords with bcrypt." Before you nod — what has that sentence NOT told you about whether authentication is actually secure? Answer before reading on.
identity-authentication.reveal: It described credential verification and said nothing about the invariant. It is silent on: what proves identity AFTER login (the session/token), whether that proof can be replayed, stolen, or forged, when it expires, and what happens at the trust boundary on every subsequent request. Password hashing protects credentials at rest — one line item. The real question is: for any request, what is the exact thing an attacker must possess or forge to be accepted as someone else? If you cannot state that as an invariant, bcrypt is a padlock on an open gate.

identity-authentication.title: Authentication is a proven invariant at a trust boundary, not a login step
identity-authentication.text: Name the identity assets, draw the boundary a credential crosses, then state one falsifiable invariant: exactly what an attacker must forge to be accepted as another principal. If any request accepts identity without satisfying it, the control is broken — regardless of the login page.

identity-authentication.title: The authentication trust boundary
identity-authentication.subtitle: A credential crosses from the untrusted zone into the trusted zone exactly once at the token issuer; every later request re-crosses it carrying only a session token. The invariant lives on the verify edge — the failure path (forged/replayed token) and the repair path (verify signature + expiry + revocation) are both marked.

legend.label: the verify edge — where the invariant is enforced
abuse path the invariant must reject
source of truth + evidence (revocation, audit)

identity-authentication.title: Section 1 of the packet + the verify that enforces it
identity-authentication.subtitle: The authentication invariant written down, then the exact middleware that makes it true on every request. This is the artifact a reviewer inspects.

steps.label: Name the assets + boundary
steps.note: Identity, the session token, and the signing key are the assets. The boundary is the line between the untrusted internet and the trusted API — write it down, do not assume it.

steps.label: The invariant, as three testable conditions
steps.note: Signature-valid AND unexpired AND not-revoked. Each is falsifiable: a reviewer can craft a request that violates exactly one and confirm rejection.

steps.label: The abuse case that anchors it
steps.note: A replayed logged-out token is the realistic OWASP-class attack (broken authentication / identification). The invariant exists to reject THIS request.

steps.label: Verify signature + expiry
steps.note: verify() rejects a forged or tampered token; the exp check rejects a stale one. Two of the three conditions, both fail-closed (throw, never fall through).

steps.label: Check revocation — the line beginners skip
steps.note: Signature + expiry alone accept a stolen token until it expires. The revocation check against the session store is what makes logout and "kill this session" real.

steps.label: Audit the decision, then return the minimal principal
steps.note: Every accept/reject is written to the append-only audit log (your abuse-case evidence). The returned principal carries only the id + session — least privilege starts here.

identity-authentication.caption: A reviewer should be able to hand-craft a request that violates each of (a), (b), (c) and watch it get rejected — that IS the proof, not the login demo.

identity-authentication.title: Weak vs gold: two claims of "we do authentication"
identity-authentication.subtitle: Same login form. Only one is a control an attacker cannot walk through.

left.label: Weak — a login page
lines: "Users log in; we bcrypt the password"
No stated invariant — auth = the login step
Token checked for signature only, never revocation
Logout clears the cookie client-side; token still valid
No audit log — a replay leaves no trace
Cannot produce a request that SHOULD be rejected
left.verdict: Vulnerable: OWASP broken-authentication by construction

right.label: Gold — a proven invariant
lines: Invariant written: signature AND expiry AND not-revoked
Named boundary: untrusted internet -> trusted API
Every request re-verifies; revocation checked server-side
Logout revokes the session id in the store — token dies
Every auth decision hits the append-only audit log
A failing unauthorized request is shown, with log evidence
right.verdict: Provable: least privilege, replay-denied, audited

identity-authentication.caption: The gap is not the login form — both have one. It is whether you can name the invariant, deny a concrete abuse case, and point to the audit-log line that proves it. Vague vocabulary caps this lesson; a failing unauthorized request unlocks it.

identity-authentication.text: Grounding in OWASP: "Identification and Authentication Failures" (A07) is a Top 10 category precisely because teams verify credentials at login and then trust the token forever. The senior tell is the revocation check — signature + expiry is what everyone writes; server-side revocation on every request is what makes logout, session-theft response, and forced re-auth actually work. If your token cannot be killed before it expires, you do not have sessions, you have time bombs.

identity-authentication.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence this authentication is not just a happy-path login." Which response proves the control?
options: "We hash passwords with bcrypt and use HTTPS, so credentials are protected."
"Here is a request replaying a logged-out user's token; it returns 401 because the session id is revoked, and here is the audit-log line recording the rejected attempt."
"Our login page has been in production for a year with no reported issues."
"We use JWTs, and JWTs are signed, so they cannot be forged."
identity-authentication.explanation: Only option 2 points to the four pieces the reviewer challenge demands: the abuse case (replayed logged-out token), the failing unauthorized request (401), the invariant that caused it (revocation check), and audit-log evidence. bcrypt (1) protects credentials at rest but says nothing about session replay; "no reported issues" (3) is absence of evidence; "JWTs are signed" (4) ignores expiry and revocation — a signed token stolen after logout is still signature-valid.

identity-authentication.intro: Prove the invariant holds — no vibes:
items: Read your invariant aloud. If it says "users log in" instead of stating exactly what a request must carry to be accepted as a principal, it is a feature description — rewrite it as a testable claim.
Craft a request that violates each condition in turn — bad signature, expired token, revoked session — and confirm each is rejected (fail-closed, not fall-through).
Log out, then replay the pre-logout token against a protected endpoint. If it is accepted, revocation is not wired — that is the abuse case, un-repaired.
Open the audit log after the replay attempt. If the rejected request left no line, you have no evidence and no detection — add it.
Confirm the returned principal carries only what downstream authorization needs (least privilege), not the whole user record or elevated claims.

prompts: In your own words: what is the difference between verifying a credential at login and enforcing an authentication invariant on every request?
Explain why signature + expiry is not enough, using your own session store and the logout-replay abuse case as the example.
Point to the exact audit-log line that proves your control rejected an unauthorized request — and say what a reviewer would conclude if that line were missing.

identity-authentication.text: The move is domain-independent: name the assets, draw the boundary, state the invariant, deny an abuse case, prove it, audit it. A payments gateway proves "only the cardholder's authenticated session can initiate a charge"; a hospital system proves "only an authenticated clinician on-shift can open a chart" — same packet, different assets and abuse cases. What stays invariant is the shape; what changes with scale, risk, and privacy is how strong the proof must be (a one-way door like a funds transfer demands MFA + short-lived tokens; a two-way door tolerates less). This same threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md is the artifact the security capstone reuses — the next lesson takes the principal you just authenticated and adds Section 2, Authorization: turning "who are you" into "what may you do," enforced under least privilege with its own abuse case and failing-request proof.

session-token-security.outcome: Take one real session-token surface (a login that mints a token, a cookie that carries it, a middleware that trusts it) and produce threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: the token's assets and trust boundary, the controls that keep it unforgeable and non-replayable, a named abuse case, and the failing unauthorized request that proves the control holds.
session-token-security.proof: threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger, containing: the token's contents and lifetime, the trust boundary it crosses, the control set (signature, expiry, revocation, transport flags), one abuse case (steal/replay/forge), the exact unauthorized request that now returns 401, and an audit-log line proving the denial was recorded. A reviewer can replay the abuse case and watch it fail.
session-token-security.unlock: Your packet names the assets and boundary, states the invariant (a token is only trusted if it is unforgeable, unexpired, and not revoked), and shows a real unauthorized request being denied and logged.
session-token-security.doNotClaim: Do not claim the token is secure because it 'has a signature'. A signed token with no expiry, no revocation, and a readable secret in the repo is a forever-valid bearer credential. Security is the whole invariant enforced and proven, not one property asserted.

session-token-security.text: An attacker copies one session cookie out of a logged browser, pastes it into curl from another continent, and the API answers as if they were the user. Nothing was 'hacked' — the token was simply believed.

A session token is the thing your whole app trusts AFTER login — every request rides on it, so if it can be forged, stolen, or replayed, authentication is over. This lesson sits in the Security & Identity foundation: it hardens the credential that authorization, object access, and audit logging all stand on.

session-token-security.prompt: Your JWT is signed with HS256 and the signature verifies on every request. Is the session secure? Decide before reading on.
session-token-security.reveal: No — verifying a signature only proves the token was minted by someone holding the secret; it says nothing about WHO is holding the token now. A signed token with no expiry never dies; with no revocation you cannot log anyone out; over HTTP or without HttpOnly it is trivially stolen; and if the HS256 secret sits in the repo, an attacker forges their own. The invariant is unforgeable AND unexpired AND not-revoked AND not-stealable — a valid signature is one of four, and the other three are where real breaches live.

session-token-security.title: A session token is trusted only if it is unforgeable, unexpired, not revoked, and not stealable
session-token-security.text: The token is a bearer credential: whoever holds it is treated as the user. So the control set must hold four properties at once — a signature the client cannot forge, a short expiry, a server-side revocation check, and transport flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) that stop theft. Drop any one and the whole session is compromisable.

session-token-security.title: The session-token trust boundary and where it breaks
session-token-security.subtitle: Login mints a token; every later request replays it across the trust boundary. Four attacks (forge, steal, replay, no-logout) hit four controls. The stolen-cookie path and the revocation gate are the suspect edges.

session-token-security.title: The gold session control, one line at a time
session-token-security.subtitle: Mint with a short exp + jti, set theft-proof cookie flags, and verify signature AND expiry AND revocation on every request.

steps.label: Secret lives in env, never in source
steps.note: If the HS256 secret is committed, an attacker forges their own valid tokens — signature verification becomes worthless. This is the 'unforgeable' property; it rests entirely on secrecy of the key.

steps.label: jti + short expiry make revocation and replay-capping possible
steps.note: The jti is a unique handle so a single session can be killed; expiresIn: '15m' bounds how long a stolen token is useful. A token with no exp is a forever-valid bearer credential.

steps.label: Cookie flags stop theft at the transport layer
steps.note: HttpOnly defeats XSS cookie theft, Secure defeats network sniffing, SameSite=Strict defeats CSRF replay. These are the 'not stealable' property — the most common real-world miss.

steps.label: Verify checks signature AND expiry together
steps.note: jwt.verify rejects a forged signature and an expired token. Pinning algorithms:['HS256'] blocks the alg:none / algorithm-confusion forgery class.

steps.label: Revocation is the fourth control most apps skip
steps.note: Without a revocation check, 'log out' and 'we were breached, kill all sessions' do nothing until every token naturally expires. This line is what makes logout real.

session-token-security.caption: Four properties, one path: unforgeable (secret + pinned alg), unexpired (exp), not revoked (jti check), not stealable (cookie flags). Miss one and the abuse case below succeeds.

session-token-security.text: OWASP API Top 10 lists Broken Authentication (API2) precisely because teams verify the signature and stop. The senior tell is the revocation store: if you cannot answer 'how do I instantly invalidate one stolen session without rotating the secret and logging everyone out?', your logout is cosmetic and your breach response is 'wait 15 minutes and hope'.

session-token-security.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this session control is not just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually proves it?
options: 'The JWT library verifies the signature, so forged tokens are rejected.'
'Here is a request with a tampered token returning 401, a request with an expired token returning 401, and a revoked-session request returning 401 — each with the matching audit-log line.'
'We use HTTPS and HttpOnly cookies, so tokens cannot be stolen.'
'The token payload is base64-encoded, so attackers cannot read it.'
session-token-security.explanation: Proof is a failing unauthorized request plus its audit trail across each control, not an asserted property. Option 1 covers only forgery (one of four); option 3 asserts a control without demonstrating the deny; option 4 confuses encoding with security (JWT payloads are readable by design). Only option 2 shows tamper, expiry, and revocation each producing a logged 401 — the exact abuse-case-denied evidence the packet requires.

session-token-security.intro: Prove the session control holds — abuse case, denied, and logged:
items: Tamper test: flip one character of a valid token and send it. It must return 401 (signature check), and the denial must appear in the audit log with the reason.
Expiry test: use a token past its exp. It must return 401 (not a 200), proving expiry is enforced, not just embedded.
Revocation test: log out (or add the jti to the revocation store), then replay the previously-valid token. It must now return 401 — proving logout is real, not cosmetic.
Theft-flag check: inspect the Set-Cookie header and confirm HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite are all present — the transport controls that stop the stolen-cookie path.
Secret check: grep the repo and history for the signing secret. If it is anywhere in source, the token is forgeable and the whole control fails regardless of the tests above.

lines: Signed token, but no exp -> valid forever
No jti / no revocation store -> logout does nothing
Cookie set without HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite -> stealable via XSS + sniffing
algorithms not pinned -> alg-confusion forgery possible
Signing secret committed to the repo
Proof = 'the signature verifies' (one of four properties)

right.label: Gold — full invariant, proven
lines: Short exp (15m) -> bounded replay window
jti + revocation store -> instant per-session kill-switch
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict -> theft + CSRF blocked

session-token-security.caption: The gap is not the library — it is the three controls beyond the signature (expiry, revocation, transport flags) and the evidence that each denies a real abuse case.

session-token-security.text: The invariant travels to every bearer credential you will ever secure: API keys, OAuth access + refresh tokens, password-reset links, signed download URLs. What stays invariant is the four-part test — unforgeable, unexpired, revocable, unstealable — and the proof shape: name the abuse case, show the denied request, keep the audit line. What changes is the surface: a refresh token needs rotation-on-use and reuse-detection; a reset link is single-use; a machine API key needs scoping and rotation instead of cookie flags. This packet is capstone evidence: the security capstone reuses threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md as the session-hardening exhibit — your portfolio claim is 'here is a session control I threat-modeled, attacked, and proved denies replay,' not 'I know about JWTs.'

authorization-rbac-abac.outcome: Take one real cross-boundary action (e.g. GET /tenants/{id}/invoices) and produce the access-control section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: the asset, the trust boundary, an RBAC role check AND the ABAC attribute check it misses, plus the one abuse case that defeats roles-only.
authorization-rbac-abac.proof: The access-control section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: named asset + trust boundary, an access matrix (role × action), the ABAC predicate that enforces ownership/tenancy, and a failing unauthorized request captured from the deny path. A reviewer can point to the exact line that stops user A from reading tenant B's invoice.
authorization-rbac-abac.unlock: Your packet names the asset and boundary, encodes least privilege as a matrix, and enforces the resource-scoping attribute (owner/tenant) that RBAC alone cannot express.
authorization-rbac-abac.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'authorization' because a role check passes. `hasRole('billing_reader')` answers 'what may this ROLE do', never 'may THIS user touch THIS row'. A packet with roles but no ownership/tenant predicate is a horizontal-privilege escalation (OWASP BOLA) waiting to happen — not authorization.

authorization-rbac-abac.text: The audit log shows a 200, not a 403: user A, a legitimate 'billing_reader', pulled tenant B's invoices — same role, wrong tenant. The role check passed; nothing checked whose data it was. That single missing attribute is the most-exploited API flaw on the OWASP API Top 10.

Authentication proved WHO is calling; authorization decides WHAT they may touch — and it is the boundary attackers actually cross. This lesson turns that boundary into a reviewable packet: RBAC for coarse capability, ABAC for the row-level 'is this yours' check, with an abuse case and audit-log proof.

authorization-rbac-abac.prompt: Your endpoint checks `if (!user.hasRole('billing_reader')) return 403`. Two users both have that role. What can still go catastrophically wrong? Answer before reading on.
authorization-rbac-abac.reveal: Horizontal privilege escalation — BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization), OWASP API #1. The role says 'this user may read invoices', never 'this user may read THIS invoice'. User A (tenant 42) requests /invoices/9001 belonging to tenant 88; the role check passes because both are 'billing_reader'. RBAC scopes by ROLE; the missing dimension is the OBJECT's attributes (owner_id, tenant_id) vs the subject's. That row-level predicate is exactly what ABAC adds — and its absence is the single most common real-world authorization breach.

authorization-rbac-abac.title: RBAC scopes the verb; ABAC scopes the object
authorization-rbac-abac.text: RBAC grants capabilities to roles (billing_reader may read invoices). ABAC decides on attributes at request time (subject.tenant == resource.tenant). The invariant: least privilege needs BOTH — role for the action, attribute predicate for the specific row. Roles alone can't say 'yours'.

authorization-rbac-abac.title: The authorization decision path — where roles pass and attributes must catch
authorization-rbac-abac.subtitle: Request crosses the tenant trust boundary. RBAC answers 'may this role read invoices?' (yes). ABAC answers 'is invoice 9001 THIS caller's?' (no) — the deny path plus its audit-log entry is the whole lesson.

steps.label: RBAC — deny-by-default
steps.note: The cheap coarse gate: absent the role, deny and log. This is necessary but NOT sufficient — both attackers here HAVE the role. Never stop at this line.

steps.label: ABAC — the ownership predicate
steps.note: subject.tenantId !== invoice.tenantId is the check RBAC structurally cannot make: it compares SUBJECT attributes to OBJECT attributes at request time. This is the least-privilege boundary.

steps.label: The deny path is the deliverable
steps.note: User A (tenant 42) → invoice (tenant 88): 42 ≠ 88 → 403, logged with both tenant IDs. That audit line is the evidence a reviewer inspects for the abuse case.

steps.label: Allow only on match, and log it
steps.note: Every decision — allow and deny — is written to the audit log. No silent grants; the log is your regression signal and incident evidence.

authorization-rbac-abac.caption: Run the abuse case: forge subject{tenant:42} against invoice{tenant:88}. Correct code returns 403 + an abac.cross_tenant log line. If it returns 200, you shipped BOLA.

authorization-rbac-abac.text: OWASP grounding (API Security Top 10): API1 Broken Object Level Authorization is the #1 API risk precisely because RBAC-only code looks correct in review — the role check is right there. The tell reviewers are trained to demand: 'show me where the OBJECT's owner is compared to the CALLER's identity.' No object-level predicate = no authorization, regardless of how many roles you defined.

authorization-rbac-abac.question: A reviewer says: 'Your role checks are clean, but I can still read another tenant's data.' What is the exact defect and its fix?
options: Missing authentication — add a login check before the endpoint.

Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA): RBAC scopes the action but never compares the object's owner/tenant to the caller's; add an ABAC predicate (subject.tenant == resource.tenant) evaluated on the loaded resource.
The role names are wrong — rename 'billing_reader' to 'tenant_billing_reader'.
Rate limiting is missing — throttle the endpoint to slow the attacker down.
authorization-rbac-abac.explanation: The reviewer's symptom — same role, wrong tenant, still allowed — is textbook BOLA (OWASP API#1). Authentication (1) is already present; the caller is known. Renaming (3) and rate limiting (4) change nothing about the decision. The only fix is a row-level attribute check comparing the resource's tenant/owner to the subject's, evaluated after the resource loads — exactly the ABAC predicate RBAC cannot express.

authorization-rbac-abac.title: Roles-only vs role + attribute predicate
authorization-rbac-abac.subtitle: Same endpoint, same authenticated user with the correct role. Only one survives the cross-tenant abuse case.

left.label: RBAC only (weak)
lines: if (!hasRole('billing_reader')) return 403
return invoice   // whichever id was asked for
Answers 'may this role read invoices' — yes
Never compares invoice.tenant to caller.tenant
Abuse: A(tenant 42) reads invoice(tenant 88) → 200
Audit log shows a legitimate-looking success
left.verdict: BOLA — horizontal privilege escalation ships

right.label: RBAC + ABAC (gold)
lines: Role gate first (deny-by-default, cheap)
THEN subject.tenantId !== invoice.tenantId → 403
Least privilege: read only your own tenant's rows
Abuse case: 42 ≠ 88 → 403 + abac.cross_tenant log
Deny path is tested, not assumed
Audit log is the incident + regression evidence
right.verdict: Least privilege enforced at the object level

authorization-rbac-abac.caption: The whole gap is one predicate. RBAC decides the verb; ABAC decides the noun. Ship both, and prove the deny path with a failing unauthorized request.

authorization-rbac-abac.intro: Prove the packet holds — no happy-path vibes:
items: Fire the abuse case: a valid subject with the right role but the WRONG tenant against a real resource id. It must return 403, not 200. If it returns the data, you have BOLA — stop and fix.
Grep the audit log for the deny: an abac.cross_tenant entry with both the subject tenant and object tenant recorded. No log line = no evidence.
Confirm the access matrix (role × action) exists in the packet AND that at least one cell is a deny the ABAC predicate enforces — roles alone must not be able to reach it.
Check deny-by-default: remove the role and the request denies; remove the ABAC check and the cross-tenant abuse case now PASSES (this is the mutation that must break the test).
Have a peer point to the exact line that stops user A from reading tenant B's invoice. If they can't find it in five seconds, the object-level check isn't there.

Explain the division of labor — what does RBAC decide, what does ABAC decide — using your own endpoint's asset and tenant boundary as the example.
Point to the one line in your artifact that enforces least privilege at the row level, and state the abuse case it defeats plus the audit-log entry that proves it.

authorization-rbac-abac.text: The same pattern scopes any resource behind any boundary: a doc-sharing app (role 'editor' + ABAC 'is this doc in a workspace you belong to'), a healthcare API (role 'clinician' + ABAC 'is this patient assigned to you' — the break-glass exception logged as its own event), cloud IAM (an S3 policy where the role grants s3:GetObject but a condition key pins the object's tenant tag to the principal). Invariant: RBAC for the verb, an attribute predicate for the specific object, deny-by-default, audit every decision. What changes is the attribute — owner, tenant, assignment, classification, time-of-day. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md forward: it is the exact artifact the security capstone reuses — the same asset, trust boundary, access matrix, abuse case, and audit-log proof plug straight into the threat model, exploit regression, and IAM policy. Not 'I understand authorization' but 'here is the request I denied, and the log line that proves it.'

object-level-authorization.outcome: Take one real endpoint that returns a user-owned object by ID (e.g. GET /api/invoices/:id) and write the object-level authorization section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: the asset, the trust boundary the request crosses, the ownership check that must run BEFORE the object is returned, the exact unauthorized request that must be denied, and the audit-log line that proves the denial.
object-level-authorization.proof: The object-level-authorization section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: a named asset, a per-object ownership predicate stated as code or pseudocode, one concrete IDOR request (attacker's token, victim's object id), the expected 403/404, and a matching audit-log entry (who, what object, allow|deny). A reviewer can replay the unauthorized request and see it denied.
object-level-authorization.unlock: Your packet names the object, states the ownership check that runs before data is returned, and shows one unauthorized request being denied with an audit-log line.
object-level-authorization.doNotClaim: Do not claim object-level authorization exists because the user is authenticated. Authentication proves WHO is calling; authorization proves they may touch THIS object. A logged-in user reading another user's invoice by changing the id is still a full breach — 'they had a valid token' is the excuse in the incident report, not the defense.

object-level-authorization.text: A logged-in customer opens their invoice — GET /api/invoices/8842 — then, on a hunch, changes 8842 to 8843. Someone else's invoice loads: name, address, card last-four. No error, no alert. They just walked through a door the code forgot to lock, and OWASP calls it the number-one API risk for a reason.

Every request that fetches a user-owned object by ID crosses a trust boundary: the attacker controls the ID. Object level authorization is the check that the caller may touch THIS specific object — the missing check behind Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), OWASP API Security #1.

object-level-authorization.prompt: Your endpoint requires a valid login token and runs SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = :id. It is authenticated. Is it safe? Answer before reading on.
object-level-authorization.reveal: No — it is authenticated but not authorized. The token proves the caller is a real user; nothing checks that invoice :id belongs to that user. Change the id to a value you do not own and the row comes back anyway. The missing clause is the whole vulnerability: WHERE id = :id AND owner_id = :caller. This is the 'oh!' — authentication and object-level authorization are different gates, and passing the first tells you nothing about the second.

object-level-authorization.title: Authorize the object, not just the caller — deny by default
object-level-authorization.text: For every object fetched by a caller-supplied ID, verify THIS caller owns THIS object before returning it. The invariant: the ownership predicate runs server-side on the object's real owner, never on a trusted client claim. No match means 404/403 — deny by default.

object-level-authorization.title: Where BOLA lives: the ownership check on the request path
object-level-authorization.subtitle: Attacker holds a valid token but swaps the object id. The gate that must catch it is the per-object ownership check between the handler and the datastore — not the auth middleware.

legend.label: the object-level authorization gate (the whole skill)
attack path + the deny that stops it
authentication — proves WHO, not WHICH object

object-level-authorization.title: The ownership predicate, one line at a time
object-level-authorization.subtitle: The gold handler from the packet: deny by default, filter by owner in the query, log both outcomes.

steps.label: Caller from the token, not the request
steps.note: callerId comes from the verified token. If it came from the body or a query param, the attacker sets it themselves — that is a BOLA by construction.

steps.label: Attacker-controlled input
steps.note: invoiceId is fully controlled by the caller. Every value here is a guess an attacker can iterate — sequential IDs make it trivial.

steps.label: The ownership predicate
steps.note: id AND ownerId in the same WHERE. The database enforces ownership; the object never loads unless it is the caller's. This one clause is the fix.

steps.label: Deny by default, 404 not 403
steps.note: No row means deny. Return 404, not 403 — a 403 confirms the object exists and leaks enumeration signal. Log the deny with actor + object.

steps.label: Log the allow too
steps.note: Both outcomes are audited. The allow trail is what proves, later, that access was legitimate — and the deny trail is what a detection rule alarms on.

object-level-authorization.caption: The whole control is one WHERE clause plus deny-by-default. Swap the id to a victim's and findFirst returns null → 404 → audited DENY.

object-level-authorization.title: Weak vs gold: same endpoint, one clause apart
object-level-authorization.subtitle: GET /api/invoices/:id. Both authenticate. Only one authorizes the object.

left.label: Weak — authenticated but IDOR-open
lines: where: { id: invoiceId }  — no owner filter
Trusts the token to mean 'may read anything'
Sequential IDs → attacker enumerates every invoice
Returns 403 on cross-tenant → confirms object exists
No audit line, so the breach is invisible after the fact
left.verdict: Broken Object Level Authorization — OWASP API #1

right.label: Gold — object-scoped, deny by default
lines: where: { id: invoiceId, ownerId: callerId }
callerId from verified token, never from input
Cross-tenant id → null → 404 (no existence leak)
Allow AND deny both written to the audit log
Replayable IDOR request denied under test
right.verdict: Least privilege enforced per object, and proven

object-level-authorization.caption: The gap between a breach and a control is one WHERE clause plus a deny-by-default default. Enforce ownership in the query, not in a client claim.

object-level-authorization.text: OWASP API Security Top 10 ranks Broken Object Level Authorization #1 because it is the most common and most damaging API flaw — one unchecked ID exposes every record. The pro move: never authorize with a claim the client controls (userId in the body, tenant in a header). Resolve the caller server-side from the token, and enforce ownership in the datastore query so a missed check fails closed, not open.

object-level-authorization.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this isn't just a happy-path answer.' Which response proves object-level authorization is actually enforced?
options: The endpoint requires a valid JWT, so only logged-in users can reach it.
A replayed request — attacker's token, victim's object id — returns 404, and the audit log shows a matching DENY line for actor+object.
The code review passed and the function has unit tests for the happy path.
The response returns 403 Forbidden when a user requests another user's invoice.
object-level-authorization.explanation: Only option 2 proves the control end-to-end: a concrete unauthorized request (cross-owner IDOR) is denied AND the denial is evidenced in the audit log. Option 1 is authentication, not object authorization. Option 3 tests only the happy path — the exact case BOLA hides in. Option 4 denies but leaks existence: 403 confirms the object is real, aiding enumeration; 404 is the safer deny.

object-level-authorization.intro: Prove the object-level authorization control — no vibes:
items: Replay the exact IDOR: caller A's token requesting caller B's object id. It must return 404 (or 403) and never leak B's data.
Confirm the caller identity comes from the verified token, not from any request-controlled field (body userId, X-Tenant header, query param).
Confirm ownership is enforced in the datastore query (WHERE id AND owner), so a forgotten check fails closed, not open.
Confirm the audit log records both allow and deny with actor, object, action, and result — and that the denied attempt appears.
Add the failing unauthorized request to a regression test so the exploit stays dead on the next deploy.

prompts: In your own words: why does a valid authentication token prove nothing about whether the caller may read THIS object?
Explain the difference between authorizing the caller and authorizing the object, using your own endpoint as the example.
Why return 404 instead of 403 on a cross-owner request, and what enumeration signal does 403 leak?
Walk through the exact IDOR request against your endpoint and name the line of code that denies it.

object-level-authorization.text: The same invariant governs every object fetched by a caller-supplied handle — not just invoices. A messaging app authorizes message_id against the conversation's members; a hospital system authorizes chart_id against the treating clinician; multi-tenant SaaS authorizes every row against tenant_id, never a client-sent tenant header. What stays invariant: resolve the caller server-side, enforce ownership in the query, deny by default, audit both outcomes. What changes with scale: a shared-object case (a doc shared with N users) swaps the single owner check for a membership/ACL lookup — still server-side, still fail-closed. This packet section — asset, ownership predicate, denied IDOR request, and audit line — is reused directly in the security capstone's access-control matrix and its exploit-regression suite: the capstone replays your unauthorized request and expects the same DENY.

input-validation-injection.outcome: Take one real endpoint that crosses an authorization boundary and write the Input Validation Injection section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: the untrusted inputs, the allow-list schema that accepts only known-good shapes, the injection sink each input reaches, and the parameterized control that denies the exploit.
input-validation-injection.proof: The Input Validation section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: named assets + trust boundary, an allow-list schema (not a deny-list), the injection sink per input (SQL / shell / template / path), a parameterized control, and one failing malicious request proving the exploit is denied. A reviewer can point at the audit-log line where the abuse case was rejected.
input-validation-injection.unlock: Your section validates input against an allow-list at the trust boundary AND neutralizes the sink with parameterization — and a malicious request is denied with audit-log evidence.
input-validation-injection.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'validated input' because you blocklisted a few bad characters. A deny-list is a guess about every attack you did not think of. Validation means an allow-list of known-good structure; injection defense means the untrusted value never reaches an interpreter as code.

input-validation-injection.text: A single order-lookup endpoint takes ?id= straight into a string-built SQL query. One reviewer types id=0 OR 1=1-- and reads every customer's orders — no exploit kit, no zero-day, just input that was trusted to be an integer and wasn't.

Injection is OWASP's oldest survivor because every app has a trust boundary where external strings meet an interpreter — SQL, a shell, a template, a file path. This lesson turns 'we validate input' into a reviewable control in threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md, the same artifact the security capstone reuses.

input-validation-injection.prompt: An endpoint escapes single quotes in the user's search term before building the SQL string. Is that input now safe from SQL injection? Decide before reading on.
input-validation-injection.reveal: No — escaping is a deny-list in disguise, and it leaks. Numeric context needs no quotes (id=1 OR 1=1), second-order injection stores the value and detonates it later, and one missed encoding (Unicode, backslash, LIKE wildcards) reopens the hole. The invariant is not 'clean the string' — it is 'the untrusted value never reaches the interpreter as code.' Parameterized queries send data as data on a separate channel; escaping tries to out-clever the parser and eventually loses.

input-validation-injection.title: Validate at the boundary, parameterize at the sink
input-validation-injection.text: Two controls, not one. At the trust boundary: an allow-list schema accepts only known-good shape and rejects the rest. At the injection sink: parameterization sends the value as data, never as code. Deny-lists and escaping are guesses; both controls together deny the class.

input-validation-injection.title: Where untrusted input meets an interpreter
input-validation-injection.subtitle: A request crosses the trust boundary into the API. Validated once against an allow-list, the value fans out to four sinks. The unvalidated path (dashed) reaches the SQL interpreter as code — the injection. Payments is out of scope.

legend.label: attacker-controlled / injection path
the trust boundary (validate here)
sink neutralized (parameterized)

input-validation-injection.title: The weak-to-gold fix, one line at a time
input-validation-injection.subtitle: The vulnerable order-lookup, then the allow-list schema + parameterized query that denies it. This block is the artifact's core evidence.

steps.label: The vulnerable trust
steps.note: req.query.id is an untrusted string treated as an integer. No validation — the boundary does not exist yet.

steps.label: The injection sink
steps.note: String interpolation makes the input part of the SQL text. id=0 OR 1=1-- turns the WHERE into always-true and dumps the table. This is the OWASP A03 injection.

steps.label: Validate at the boundary
steps.note: The Zod schema is an allow-list: coerce to integer, must be positive, else parse() throws before any query runs. Unknown shapes are rejected by construction, not by guessing at bad characters.

steps.label: Parameterize at the sink
steps.note: $1 is a bind placeholder — the driver sends id on a separate channel, so 0 OR 1=1 can only ever be the literal value, never code. The sink is neutralized even if validation were bypassed.

steps.label: Least privilege in the query
steps.note: AND owner_id = $2 enforces object-level authorization: even a valid id returns nothing unless the caller owns it. Defense in depth — validation, parameterization, and access control stacked.

steps.label: Audit-log the decision
steps.note: Every access records actor + resource + allowed. This line is the evidence a reviewer inspects to prove the abuse case was denied, not just that the happy path worked.

input-validation-injection.caption: Run the malicious request against the gold version: id='0 OR 1=1--' fails Zod parse with a 400 before the DB is touched — the audit log shows the rejection, not a data dump.

input-validation-injection.title: Blocklist-and-escape vs allow-list-and-parameterize
input-validation-injection.subtitle: Same endpoint, same attacker. One control class guesses at attacks; the other denies the whole class.

left.label: Deny-list + escape (weak)
lines: Strips quotes and the word DROP from input
No schema — any shape passes if it looks clean
Numeric context (id=1 OR 1=1) needs no quotes → bypass
Second-order: stored value detonates on a later query
One missed encoding (Unicode, \\, LIKE %) reopens it
No object-level check — valid id reads anyone's order
left.verdict: Guesses every attack you didn't think of — and loses one

right.label: Allow-list + parameterize (gold)
lines: Zod schema: id must be a positive integer, else 400
Untrusted value bound as $1 — data, never code
Numeric and string injection both structurally impossible
owner_id = $2 enforces least privilege at the row
Audit log records the denied abuse case as evidence
Same control ports to shell (argv) and templates (auto-escape)
right.verdict: Denies the injection class, not one payload

input-validation-injection.caption: The deny-list defends against the last attack; the allow-list defends against the next one. Parameterization removes the sink so the question 'did I escape everything?' stops mattering.

input-validation-injection.text: OWASP A03:2021 folds Injection and XSS into one category for a reason: the fix is identical across sinks — keep untrusted data out of the interpreter's code channel. SQL gets bind parameters, the shell gets an argv array (never a shell string), templates get context-aware auto-escaping, file paths get canonicalization inside a confined root. Different interpreter, same invariant.

input-validation-injection.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this isn't just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually proves the injection control holds?
options: 'The endpoint has input validation and the tests pass.'
'I added a Zod schema, so malformed input is rejected.'
'Here is the failing request id=0 OR 1=1-- returning 400 at the boundary, the parameterized query, and the audit-log line showing the abuse case was denied.'
'We escape single quotes and strip SQL keywords from every parameter.'
input-validation-injection.explanation: The reviewer challenge demands the artifact, the broken case, the proof output, and the control together. Only option 3 points at the denied malicious request AND the audit-log evidence AND the parameterized sink. Option 1 is a vibe, option 2 shows only half the control (boundary, not sink), and option 4 is the deny-list this lesson exists to kill — it fails on numeric and second-order injection.

input-validation-injection.intro: Prove the control holds — no vibes:
items: Validation is an allow-list: your schema names the accepted shape and rejects everything else, not a blocklist of bad characters.
Every untrusted input is traced to its sink (SQL / shell / template / path), and each sink is parameterized or context-escaped — not string-built.
Run one malicious request per sink (id=0 OR 1=1--, ; rm -rf, {{7*7}}, ../../etc/passwd). Each is denied at the boundary or rendered inert at the sink.
Object-level authorization is enforced in the query itself (owner_id = $actor), so a valid-but-unauthorized id returns nothing.
The audit log records actor, resource, and allowed=false for the denied abuse case — that line is the evidence you hand the reviewer.
Re-run after the repair (the retest): the previously-passing exploit now fails, and the legitimate request still succeeds.

input-validation-injection.text: The pattern is invariant across every interpreter: keep untrusted data out of the code channel, validate its shape at the boundary, enforce least privilege at the resource. It ports to LDAP filters (bind, don't concatenate), NoSQL operators (reject $-prefixed keys), OS commands (argv, never a shell string), and prompt injection into an LLM (structured tool schemas, not raw string concatenation). What stays invariant is the trust boundary and the sink; what changes is the interpreter and the escaping context. Carry this section forward: the security capstone reuses threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md — its threat model cites this injection asset, its exploit-regression test is your failing malicious request, and its IAM policy is the owner_id least-privilege check. You do not just describe input validation now. You can prove an exploit is denied.

secrets-management.unlock: Your packet names the secret as an asset, marks the trust boundary it crosses, enforces least privilege in an access matrix, and shows audit-log evidence that an unauthorized read is detectable.
secrets-management.doNotClaim: Do not claim you "manage secrets" because the value moved out of the code and into an env var committed to the repo, or into a plaintext .env baked into the image. Moving a plaintext secret is not securing it. The invariant is: the secret is never readable at rest by anyone outside the trust boundary, and every read is logged.

secrets-management.text: A junior grep of the git history turns up AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in a commit from eight months ago — still valid, never rotated, and the repo went public last week. Nobody can say who read it, because nothing ever logged the reads.

A secret is the credential that turns a request into authority — a DB password, an OAuth token, a signing key. Secrets Management is the applied-skill control that keeps that credential out of source, scoped by least privilege, and auditable, so a leak is both hard to cause and impossible to hide.

secrets-management.prompt: "We fixed it — the API key is no longer hardcoded, it's read from an environment variable now." Before you nod along: what did that actually change about the threat? Answer before reading on.
secrets-management.reveal: Often nothing. If that env var is set from a plaintext .env file committed to the repo, or baked into the Docker image layer, or printed in a crash dump, the secret is still readable at rest by anyone who can read the repo, pull the image, or read logs — the same blast radius as hardcoding, just harder to grep. "Not in the code" is not the invariant. "Not readable at rest outside the trust boundary, and every read audited" is. Moving a plaintext secret feels like remediation while leaving the vulnerability intact.

secrets-management.title: A secret is an asset behind a trust boundary — least privilege in, audit log out
secrets-management.text: Name the secret as an asset. It is encrypted at rest, injected only at runtime, readable only by the identities that need it (least privilege), and every read is logged. The invariant: no plaintext secret at rest outside the boundary, and no unaudited read.

secrets-management.title: The secret’s trust boundary — the leak path and the repair path
secrets-management.subtitle: Left: a plaintext secret in the repo/image is readable by anyone across the boundary (the leak path). Right: a secrets manager injects at runtime under IAM, and every GetSecretValue is audited (the repair path). The unauthorized reader is DENIED and logged.

legend.label: leak path — plaintext at rest, readable across the boundary
least-privilege access — identity-scoped read
repair path — encrypted at rest + audited reads

secrets-management.title: The control packet + the least-privilege policy that enforces it

secrets-management.code:
## Asset: orders/db-password  (secret ARN in Secrets Manager, KMS-encrypted)
## Trust boundary: only the Orders task role may read it at runtime

# Selected approach: runtime injection under a least-privilege IAM policy
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:...:secret:orders/db-password-*",
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/service": "orders" } }
}
# Rejected: plaintext value in .env committed to repo (readable at rest, no audit)

## Abuse case: the billing service (or a leaked repo) tries to read orders/db-password
$ aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id orders/db-password  # as billing role
AccessDeniedException: not authorized to perform secretsmanager:GetSecretValue

secrets-management.text: Grounded in OWASP (A07: Identification & Authentication Failures, and the secrets-exposure patterns behind A05: Security Misconfiguration) and the NICE Framework's least-privilege tasks: the reviewable evidence is not "we use a vault." It is the access matrix (who can read this secret) plus a captured audit event proving reads are logged. A vault with a wildcard IAM policy and audit logging turned off is theater — it has the tool and none of the invariant.

secrets-management.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this secret is actually protected, not just moved into a fancier store." Which response is the evidence?

"The secret is encrypted at rest with KMS, so it's secure."
"Only senior engineers have the vault console password."
secrets-management.explanation: The invariant is least privilege PLUS auditability, and evidence must show both the deny and the log. Option 2 proves the boundary holds (unauthorized read fails) and that reads are detectable (CloudTrail entry) — the abuse case and the audit evidence together. Migration (1) and encryption-at-rest (3) are necessary but prove neither who-can-read nor would-we-know; a broad IAM policy defeats both silently. Console access (4) is not least privilege for the service identity and logs nothing about programmatic reads.

secrets-management.intro: Prove the packet holds — no vibes:
items: The secret is named as an asset (its ARN / path), not described as "the password." If it isn't named, it can't be scoped or audited.
The IAM grant is scoped to THIS secret and THIS identity. Grep the policy for a wildcard Resource or secretsmanager:* — if you find one, least privilege is broken.
You have a CAPTURED unauthorized read that returns AccessDenied — run it as a neighbor role, not as yourself. A boundary you never watched deny anyone is unproven.
You have a CAPTURED audit-log entry for an authorized read (who / which secret / when). If reads aren't logged, a future leak is invisible — exactly the mission's failure.
No plaintext copy of the secret survives at rest: not in the repo, not in the built image layer, not in a checked-in .env. Confirm the rejected approach is actually gone, not just supplemented.

secrets-management.text: The pattern is asset → trust boundary → least privilege → audit, and it doesn't change with the secret. Swap the DB password for a Stripe signing key, a service-to-service JWT signing secret, or a customer's stored OAuth token in a multi-tenant app — the invariant holds: encrypted at rest, injected at runtime, scoped to one identity, every read logged. What changes is the blast radius and rotation urgency (a payment signing key rotates on suspicion; a tenant token is scoped per tenant so one leak can't cross the tenant boundary). This same threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md is what the Security capstone reuses — its threat model, its abuse case, its IAM policy, its detection evidence, and the incident runbook that fires when the audit log shows a read from an identity that shouldn't have one.

secure-api-design.outcome: Take one real API endpoint that returns object-scoped data (an order, an invoice, a user profile) and write the Secure API Design packet: the asset it exposes, the trust boundary a request crosses, the authorization control that enforces ownership, the abuse case that breaks the weak version, and the audit-log line that proves denial.

A reviewer runs the abuse case and watches it get denied and logged.
secure-api-design.unlock: Your packet names the asset, the trust boundary, the ownership check, and shows one unauthorized request that is denied AND recorded in an audit log.
secure-api-design.doNotClaim: Do not claim the API is "secured" because it requires a valid token. Authentication proves WHO is calling; it does not prove they may touch THIS object. An endpoint that trusts the id in the URL is Broken Object Level Authorization (OWASP API1) — authenticated and still wide open.

secure-api-design.text: You ship GET /api/orders/{id} behind a login. It works, tests pass, you deploy. Two weeks later a customer increments their order id by one in the browser bar and reads a stranger's shipping address — you authenticated the caller but never asked whether this caller owns that order.

Secure API design sits in the applied phase of Security & Identity: it turns identity and sessions into enforced authorization at every object boundary. It is the artifact the capstone reuses — the threat model, access matrix, and exploit regression that prove a control actually denies abuse, not just that a token was present.

secure-api-design.prompt: The endpoint requires a valid session token and returns the order for the id in the URL. A logged-in user changes the id to one they don't own. What stops them? Answer before reading on.
secure-api-design.reveal: Nothing. Authentication checked that the token is valid — it never checked that THIS user owns THAT order. This is Broken Object Level Authorization (OWASP API1:2023), the single most common API vulnerability. The fix is one predicate: the query must filter by the caller's identity (WHERE user_id = session.user_id AND id = :id), so a non-owner gets zero rows, not someone else's data.

secure-api-design.title: Authenticate the caller, then authorize the object — on the server, keyed on identity
secure-api-design.text: Every request crosses a trust boundary. The invariant: authorization is decided server-side from the CALLER's identity, never from an id the client sends. Trust the session, never the URL. A non-owner must get a denial, not another tenant's row.

secure-api-design.title: The trust boundary an API request crosses
secure-api-design.subtitle: The client is untrusted; the id in the URL is untrusted. Authorization must key on the session-derived caller identity and scope the query — the failure path (trusting the URL id) reads another tenant's data; the repair path denies and logs.

secure-api-design.text: The tell that separates a security-minded engineer: they never trust an identifier the client can change. Broken Object Level Authorization tops the OWASP API Security Top 10 precisely because "require a token" feels like security while every endpoint still trusts the id in the URL. Authorize the object, from the session, on the server — every time, per object, not once at the door.

A screenshot of the token being decoded successfully.
A note that the endpoint is only reachable over HTTPS.
secure-api-design.explanation: A valid-token/valid-owner test only proves authentication and the happy path — it never exercises the trust boundary. The proof of authorization is a failing unauthorized request: an authenticated non-owner denied AND recorded. Options 1, 3, and 4 all demonstrate authN or transport security, never object-level authZ — the BOLA gap stays invisible.

secure-api-design.intro: Prove the control denies abuse — no vibes:
items: Run the abuse case: as authenticated user A, request an object owned by user B. Confirm it returns a denial (404/403), not B's data.
Check the query is scoped by the caller's identity, not the URL id — grep for a WHERE that includes userId = session, not just id = param.
Confirm the denied request wrote an audit line (caller, target object, timestamp, outcome). No log line = no evidence of denial.
Confirm the identity used for authorization comes from the verified session — never a client-set header, body field, or the id itself.
Write the access matrix: for {owner, non-owner, admin} × {read, write, delete}, mark allow/deny — and confirm the code matches every cell.

secure-api-design.text: The same pattern secures any object-scoped resource, in any protocol. A GraphQL resolver must scope by the caller, not the node id the client passes. A file-download route must check the requester owns the file, not just that they're logged in. A multi-tenant SaaS must add tenant_id to every query so tenant A can never read tenant B — the ownership predicate becomes a tenancy predicate. What stays invariant: authorize the object from server-derived identity, deny by default, log the denial. What changes with scale is where the predicate lives (row-level security in the DB, a policy engine, per-tenant keys). Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the capstone — its abuse case becomes your exploit regression, its access matrix your IAM policy, its audit line your detection rule.

threat-modeling.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'threat-modeled it' if your artifact is a list of scary words (SQL injection! XSS!) with no asset, no boundary, and no denied request. A threat model without an abuse case that your control provably denies is vocabulary, not evidence. The invariant: every threat maps to an asset crossing a trust boundary, and every control has a failing unauthorized request that proves it.

threat-modeling.text: A pentester types your own user ID into someone else's invoice URL, hits enter, and your API cheerfully returns their bank details — OWASP API1, Broken Object Level Authorization, the single most-exploited API flaw on the internet. Nobody wrote that request down as a threat, so nobody built the control that stops it.

A threat model is the artifact that turns 'we should be secure' into a specific claim: this asset, crossing this trust boundary, denied by this control, proven by this failing request. It is the reviewable spine every later Security & Identity skill — access matrices, secrets, detection, incidents — hangs off of.

threat-modeling.prompt: "We use JWTs and HTTPS, so the API is secure." Before you agree — what class of attack does that sentence completely fail to address? Answer before reading on.
threat-modeling.reveal: Authorization, not authentication. JWTs prove WHO you are; HTTPS protects the bytes in transit. Neither checks whether THIS authenticated user may touch THIS object. The invoice attacker had a perfectly valid token — for their own account — and used it to read yours. That is Broken Object Level Authorization (OWASP API1), and 'we have auth' is exactly the false comfort that ships it. Authentication asks 'are you logged in?'; authorization asks 'is this yours?' — and the threat model exists to force the second question on every object.

threat-modeling.title: A threat model maps assets across trust boundaries to controls and proof
threat-modeling.text: Name the assets, draw the trust boundaries they cross, enumerate abuse cases at each boundary, assign a least-privilege control to each, and prove the control with a failing unauthorized request plus an audit log. The invariant: no control without an abuse case it provably denies.

The attacker path — a valid token requesting someone else's invoice — is marked, along with the control that denies it and the audit sink that records the attempt. Billing internals are deliberately out of scope.

threat-modeling.title: The access-control matrix + the failing request that proves it
threat-modeling.subtitle: The heart of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: a role×action matrix, the least-privilege rule, and the 403 an unauthorized request must produce.
threat-modeling.code:
# threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md — Invoice object access
# Asset: invoice (PII + bank data)  |  Boundary: object ownership
# Abuse case: user A reads user B's invoice via /invoices/{B_id}

# --- Access matrix (role x action, least privilege) ---
#   role     read_own   read_any   refund
#   owner       Y           N          N
#   support     N           Y          N
#   admin       Y           Y          Y

def authorize(user, action, invoice):
    if action == "read":
        if user.role in ("support", "admin"):
            return True                 # read_any
        return invoice.owner_id == user.id   # read_own ONLY
    raise Forbidden()

# --- Proof: the abuse case must return 403, not 200 ---
def test_bola_denied():
    victim  = Invoice(owner_id="userB")
    attacker = User(id="userA", role="owner")
    with pytest.raises(Forbidden):        # 403, and an audit line
        require(authorize(attacker, "read", victim))
    assert audit_log.last().event == "authz.denied"

steps.label: Name the asset and the abuse case
steps.note: The header IS the threat: invoice = PII + bank data, boundary = object ownership, abuse = A reads B's object. This is OWASP API1 stated concretely, not 'broken auth' in the abstract.

steps.label: The access matrix — least privilege made explicit
steps.note: role × action. 'owner' can read_own but NOT read_any — the single cell that denies the abuse. If a cell is 'Y' you cannot defend, that is a threat, not a feature.

steps.label: The control enforces the matrix per-object
steps.note: The load-bearing line is invoice.owner_id == user.id. Authn already passed; THIS is the object-level check attackers bypass when it's missing.

steps.label: The proof is a FAILING unauthorized request
steps.note: A test that can only pass is theatre. This one asserts the abuse case raises Forbidden AND writes an audit line — the two pieces of evidence the reviewer replays.

threat-modeling.caption: Run it: attacker (valid token, role owner) requests victim's invoice → Forbidden + authz.denied in the log. That 403 is the proof; without it the matrix is a wish.

threat-modeling.text: OWASP puts Broken Object Level Authorization at API1 for a reason: it's invisible to authentication tests. Every endpoint that takes an object ID in the path or body is a BOLA candidate — the senior move is to grep your routes for {id} params and ask, for each one, 'where is the owner check?' A missing owner check is a threat even when every auth test is green.

threat-modeling.text: The pattern is asset → trust boundary → abuse case → least-privilege control → failing-request proof, and it transfers to any boundary a decision crosses. A multi-tenant SaaS applies it to tenant isolation (can tenant A query tenant B's rows?); a cloud IAM policy applies it to a role assuming another role it shouldn't; a secrets store applies it to a service reading a credential outside its scope. What stays invariant: every control must have an abuse case it provably denies. What changes with scale, tenancy, or compliance: the number of boundaries and the strength of proof a reviewer demands. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the security capstone — its abuse case becomes your exploit regression, its matrix becomes your IAM policy, its audit line becomes your detection rule. That is the whole point: the artifact you built here is reused, not re-derived, downstream.

A reviewer traces one leaf-to-root path and agrees it is the cheapest way in.

A list of vulnerabilities is not a tree — the tree's whole value is showing which combinations reach the goal and which single control collapses the cheapest path. And do not claim a branch is 'defended' without an audit-log line proving the control actually fires.

attack-trees.text: The pen-test report lands with nineteen findings rated by CVSS, and the room argues for an hour about which to patch first. A staff security engineer draws one tree — attacker goal at the top — points to a single leaf where a weak reset token meets a missing rate limit, and says: "Fix this one AND-node and four of your nineteen findings become unreachable."

An attack tree turns a pile of vulnerabilities into a structured map of how an attacker actually reaches a goal — root goal, branching paths, and leaves you can price by attacker cost. It sits in the applied-skill phase of threat modeling: it is where OWASP findings and STRIDE categories become a prioritized, defendable plan for which control to build first.

attack-trees.prompt: You list five ways an attacker could take over an account and rank them by how scary each sounds. Why is "scariest first" the wrong prioritization? Answer before reading on.
attack-trees.reveal: Because the attacker doesn't pick the scariest path — they pick the cheapest one that works. Scariness is your fear; cost is their decision function. The right axis is attacker cost-to-exploit at each leaf: a $0, no-skill path (guessable 6-digit reset code with no rate limit) outranks a terrifying-but-expensive one (steal the signing key from HSM). An attack tree makes you price the leaves and defend the cheapest branch — the one they'll actually take — first.

attack-trees.title: Root goal on top, AND/OR branches down, leaves priced by attacker cost
attack-trees.text: State the attacker's goal as the root. Decompose into sub-goals: OR-nodes are alternative paths (any one succeeds), AND-nodes require every child. Leaves are concrete attack steps, each priced by cost/skill. The invariant: the tree's value is the cheapest root-reaching path — defend that first.

## Attack Tree — GOAL: take over a user account
GOAL: Attacker gains authenticated session as victim
  OR path 1: Abuse password reset            [AND — needs both leaves]
    - leaf: guess weak reset token   cost=$0  skill=low   likelihood=HIGH
    - leaf: no rate limit on /reset  cost=$0  skill=low   likelihood=HIGH
  OR path 2: Reuse leaked credential (stuffing)
    - leaf: no MFA on login          cost=$5  skill=low   likelihood=MED
- Cheapest root-reaching path: path 1 (AND of two $0/low leaves)
- Chosen control: rate-limit /reset (5/hr/account) + 128-bit token entropy
- Rejected control: CAPTCHA only (does not raise token-guess cost)
- Detection: audit_log emits reset.rate_limit.block on 6th attempt
- Reversal condition: revert if false-positive lockouts > 0.5% of resets

steps.label: Root = attacker goal, not a vuln
steps.note: The root is what the attacker WANTS ('gains authenticated session'), never a control or a CVE. Everything below is a way to get there.

steps.label: AND-node: both leaves required
steps.note: Path 1 only works if the token is guessable AND there is no rate limit. Mark it AND — because severing either child collapses the whole path. This is the leverage point.

steps.label: Price every leaf by attacker cost
steps.note: cost / skill / likelihood — the attacker's decision function, not your fear. A $0/low-skill leaf outranks a $5/med one. Least privilege reasoning starts here: which asset is cheapest to reach?

steps.label: Name the cheapest root-reaching path

attack-trees.intro: Prove your attack tree holds — no vibes:
items: The root is the attacker's GOAL (a state they want), not a vulnerability, a control, or a CVE. If it names a fix, you inverted the tree.
Every AND-node is genuinely conjunctive: severing any one child collapses that whole path. If any child alone reaches the goal, it should be an OR, not an AND.
Every leaf carries an attacker cost/skill/likelihood estimate — priced by what it costs THEM, not effort for you.
The cheapest root-reaching path is explicitly named, and the chosen control severs it (with a rejected alternative and why it costs less to defend).
There is an audit-log line (e.g. reset.rate_limit.block) proving the control actually fires on a blocked attempt — and a reversal condition if the control causes false-positive lockouts.
