secure-coding-review.doNotClaim: Do not claim a Secure Coding Review because you read the code and it 'looks fine'. A review with no abuse case, no unauthorized request, and no audit-log line is a happy-path reading. The review's job is to make the exploit fail on demand, not to vouch for the code.

secure-coding-review.text: The endpoint authenticates every caller, so the pull request is approved in two minutes — and three weeks later a customer changes /api/invoices/1001 to /api/invoices/1002 in the address bar and reads a stranger's invoice. Nobody was unauthenticated. Everybody was authorized to the wrong object.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase: earlier lessons proved identity and sessions; this one turns a diff into a reviewable authorization control. Broken Object Level Authorization (OWASP API #1 / A01 Broken Access Control) is the failure that authentication alone never catches.

secure-coding-review.prompt: A code reviewer sees `@requires_login` on the handler and a valid session on every request. The endpoint is `GET /invoices/{id}`. Is access control satisfied? Decide before reading on.
secure-coding-review.reveal: No — that only proves WHO is calling, never WHICH objects they may touch. `@requires_login` is authentication plus a door check; it says the caller is a logged-in user, not that this user owns invoice 1002. The missing invariant is object-level authorization: every object read must re-check ownership against the caller, on the object, not at the door. Authentication answers 'are you someone'; this answers 'is this yours' — and only the second one stops IDOR.

secure-coding-review.title: The invariant: authorize the object, not just the door
secure-coding-review.text: A Secure Coding Review proves each request re-checks ownership on the specific object it touches, against the authenticated caller — enforced server-side at the data boundary. Authentication at the door is necessary and never sufficient; the missing check is where IDOR lives.

A reviewer can point to the exact evidence, not a claim.
dependency-supply-chain.unlock: Your packet names the supply-chain trust boundary, shows a control that DENIES an unverified dependency, and attaches audit-log evidence of that denial.
dependency-supply-chain.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'secured the supply chain' because you ran an audit tool once and it was green. A scanner that only reports known CVEs is not a trust boundary — it cannot stop a brand-new typosquat or a signed-but-malicious update. The invariant is verified provenance at the gate, not a clean report after the fact.

dependency-supply-chain.text: A single npm postinstall script — shipped in a patch bump of a transitive dependency nobody chose — exfiltrated the CI environment's cloud credentials to an attacker's server before a human ever reviewed the diff. The code you wrote was perfect; the code you trusted was not.

Your production runtime is the sum of every package in your lockfile and every build step that assembled them — most of it written by strangers, pulled automatically, run with your privileges. Dependency Supply Chain is the discipline of turning that implicit trust into an enforced, provable boundary.

dependency-supply-chain.prompt: Your `npm audit` / `pip-audit` reports zero known vulnerabilities. Are you safe from a supply-chain attack? Answer before reading on.
dependency-supply-chain.reveal: No — you are safe from yesterday's disclosed CVEs, which is a different question. The dangerous supply-chain attacks are novel: a typosquatted package name, a maintainer account takeover pushing a malicious patch, or a build step that swaps an artifact after the scan. None of those are in a CVE database yet. A vulnerability scanner checks known-bad; a supply-chain control enforces known-good — pinned hashes and verified provenance. The green scan feels like proof and quietly answers the wrong question.

dependency-supply-chain.title: The invariant: verified provenance at the gate, not a clean scan after
dependency-supply-chain.text: Every artifact entering your build must match a pinned hash and carry provenance you verify before it runs — least privilege for code you did not write. The boundary is the install/build gate. A dependency that cannot prove what it is gets denied, and the denial is logged.

dependency-supply-chain.subtitle: A poisoned package flows registry → resolve → build → prod. The failure path (unverified artifact runs) and the repair path (pinned-hash + provenance gate DENIES, logs) are both shown.

dependency-supply-chain.title: The control packet — pin, verify, deny, log
dependency-supply-chain.subtitle: threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md paired with the CI gate that enforces it. Filled, not a template.
dependency-supply-chain.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Dependency Supply Chain gate — enforced BEFORE any install script runs.
set -euo pipefail

# 1. Install ONLY from the lockfile: exact versions + integrity hashes, no resolution.
npm ci --ignore-scripts        # postinstall scripts do NOT run yet — least privilege

# 2. Verify each package's integrity hash against the pinned lockfile.
npm audit signatures           # checks registry signatures / provenance attestations

# 3. Verify npm build provenance (SLSA attestation) for critical deps.
EXPECTED="sha512-Qm9r...pinned...=="
ACTUAL=$(node -e "process.stdout.write(require('./node_modules/left-pad/package.json').dist?.integrity ?? 'none')")
if [ "$ACTUAL" != "$EXPECTED" ]; then
  echo "DENY: left-pad integrity mismatch — expected $EXPECTED got $ACTUAL" | tee -a audit.log
  exit 1                       # fail the build — unverified artifact never runs
fi

# 4. Emit an SBOM so we can prove exactly what shipped.
npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json
echo "$(date -u +%FT%TZ) VERIFIED build sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD) sbom=sbom.json" >> audit.log

# 5. Only NOW run lifecycle scripts, on the verified tree.
npm rebuild

steps.label: Install without running code
steps.note: `npm ci` uses the lockfile's exact versions AND integrity hashes — no fresh resolution. `--ignore-scripts` denies the postinstall privilege until AFTER verification. This is the single change that stops the mission's credential-exfil attack.

steps.label: Verify provenance, not just presence
steps.note: `npm audit signatures` checks registry signatures and SLSA provenance attestations. This catches account-takeover pushes a CVE scan cannot see — known-good, not known-bad.

steps.label: The deny path
steps.note: A pinned hash mismatch is the trust boundary firing. `exit 1` fails the build — the unverified artifact never reaches production. This is the reproduced failing case your proof needs.

steps.label: The audit-log evidence
steps.note: Every denial writes to audit.log with the expected vs actual hash. This line IS the reviewer evidence — it proves the boundary denied a real artifact, not that a scan looked clean.

steps.label: SBOM — prove what shipped
steps.note: The Software Bill of Materials records every dependency + version in the verified build. Without it you cannot answer 'were we affected?' when the next registry compromise hits.

steps.label: Run scripts last, on trusted code
steps.note: Lifecycle scripts execute only after verification — least privilege enforced by ordering. Reversal condition: if a critical dep has no provenance yet, vendor + hash-pin it manually rather than dropping the gate.

dependency-supply-chain.caption: Run it against a tampered lockfile hash: the build fails at step 3 and audit.log gains a DENY line. That failing run is the deliverable, not the green one.

dependency-supply-chain.text: OWASP ranks vulnerable-and-outdated components and software/data integrity failures in its Top 10 for a reason: the highest-leverage attack is not against your code, it is against your trust. The senior tell is treating every dependency as untrusted input at a boundary — pinned, verified, inventoried in an SBOM — exactly as you would treat a user's form submission. 'It's a popular package' is not a control.

dependency-supply-chain.intro: Prove your Dependency Supply Chain control — no vibes:
items: Abuse case written: name a concrete attacker path (typosquat, maintainer takeover, or build-time swap) your gate must stop — not 'a bad package'.

cloud-iam-least-privilege.doNotClaim: Do not claim least privilege because the app still works. An app works fine with a wildcard admin role too. Least privilege is proven by a DENY on something the identity should not be able to do, captured in the audit log — not by the happy path succeeding.

cloud-iam-least-privilege.text: A leaked CI token from a single repo turns into a full account takeover — because that deployer role carried iam:* "to be safe," and iam:* means it can mint an admin for the attacker. One wildcard, one blast radius: everything.

In cloud, identity is the perimeter — there is no network edge to hide behind, only what each role is allowed to do. Least privilege is the control that turns a stolen credential from "game over" into "one narrow, logged, contained failure."

cloud-iam-least-privilege.prompt: A teammate grants a deploy role s3:* on the artifacts bucket so builds stop failing. The app works. What did they actually give away? Answer before reading on.
cloud-iam-least-privilege.reveal: Far more than "upload a build." s3:* includes DeleteObject, PutBucketPolicy, and PutBucketAcl — so a stolen deploy token can wipe every artifact, rewrite the bucket policy to make it public, or lock you out of your own bucket. The job needed exactly s3:PutObject + s3:GetObject on one prefix. "It works" told you nothing, because a wildcard always works — it just also does everything you never intended.

cloud-iam-least-privilege.title: Least privilege = the smallest allow-set that passes the abuse case
cloud-iam-least-privilege.text: Start from the abuse case, not the feature. Grant only the identity + resource + action rows the job provably needs; every other action stays denied by default. The invariant: a stolen credential can do only what the matrix justified — and the audit log proves it.

cloud-iam-least-privilege.caption: The difference is invisible on the happy path and total under attack. Least privilege is measured by what the identity is denied, not by what it can do.

cloud-iam-least-privilege.intro: Prove the packet holds — no vibes:
items: Every Allow has a matching row in the access matrix (identity x resource x action). If an action has no justifying row, delete the action, not the row.

You ran one unauthorized request (e.g. iam:CreateUser or s3:DeleteObject) with this role and captured the AccessDenied response. If it succeeded, the policy is not least-privilege — repair before unlock.
The audit log (CloudTrail / Cloud Audit Logs) shows that denied attempt as a distinct event, with the identity and action. No log line = no evidence.
The rejected over-broad option (s3:* / iam:*) is written in the packet with the specific abuse case it fails.
The resource is scoped to the narrowest ARN/prefix the job needs — a leak of this credential cannot reach a second tenant, repo, or environment.

prompts: In your own words, why does "the app still works" tell you nothing about whether a role is least-privilege?
Walk the abuse case: a token for your role leaks. Name the one action an attacker would try first, and show the exact line in your policy that denies it.
Explain the difference between the access matrix and the audit log in your packet — what does each one prove that the other cannot?

cloud-iam-least-privilege.text: The pattern is identity-agnostic. Swap the AWS deployer role for a GCP service account, a Kubernetes RBAC Role, a database grant, or an OAuth scope — the moves are invariant: name the abuse case, build the access matrix, grant only the justified actions, deny the escalation verbs explicitly, then capture a failing unauthorized request and its audit line. What changes is the surface (which verbs escalate, which resource ARN is narrowest, which log records the deny); what never changes is that least privilege is proven by a logged DENY, not a happy path. This threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md is your capstone evidence: the security capstone reuses this exact packet inside its threat model, IAM policy, detection, and runbook — the portfolio claim is not "I understand least privilege," it is "here is a role, the abuse case it denies, and the captured audit-logged proof."

network-edge-security.outcome: Take one real internet-facing service (or a realistic one) and write the edge-security section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: name the assets behind the edge, draw the trust boundary the request crosses, list the edge controls that enforce it (TLS termination, WAF ruleset, rate limit, auth at the gateway), and prove one specific abuse case is denied.
network-edge-security.proof: The 'Network Edge' section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: an asset list, one named trust boundary, the ordered controls at that boundary, a concrete abuse case, and a failing unauthorized request captured from the edge (status + which control rejected it). A reviewer can point to the exact control that denied the abuse.
network-edge-security.unlock: Your section names the trust boundary, the controls that enforce it in order, and shows one abuse request the edge rejected — with the audit-log line to prove it.
network-edge-security.doNotClaim: Do not claim the edge is 'secured' because a WAF exists. A WAF that logs but never blocks, or an allowlist the app also re-checks nowhere, is decoration. The edge is secured only when a specific abusive request returns a deny AND that denial is visible in an audit log.

network-edge-security.text: 3 a.m., the pager fires: a scraper is walking your public API, guessing object IDs, and your origin is melting because every request sails straight through to the app. The edge — the one boundary that was supposed to catch this — was a load balancer with the doors wide open.

The network edge is the first trust boundary an attacker crosses: everything before it is hostile, everything after it you are choosing to trust. Get the edge wrong and every downstream control — identity, authorization, secrets — inherits traffic that should never have arrived. This is the boundary your whole threat model stands on.

network-edge-security.prompt: "We're safe — we put the app behind a load balancer with HTTPS." Before you nod: what does that actually protect against, and what does it let straight through? Answer before reading on.
network-edge-security.reveal: Almost nothing on the attack surface. TLS encrypts the pipe — it stops eavesdropping, not abuse. A load balancer routes traffic; it does not inspect it. Credential stuffing, IDOR probes, injection payloads, and volumetric floods all ride the encrypted channel and arrive at your app looking perfectly valid. 'Behind HTTPS' answers confidentiality-in-transit and leaves authentication, rate, and input validation completely unaddressed. The edge is a control point, not just a pipe — and an uncontrolled edge is a boundary in name only.

network-edge-security.title: The edge is a trust boundary enforced by layered controls, not a pipe
network-edge-security.text: Every request crosses from untrusted to trusted at the edge. The invariant: nothing passes that boundary unless each control — TLS, WAF, rate limit, gateway auth — has had its chance to deny it. Least privilege applies to traffic, not just users: default-deny, allow the known-good.

network-edge-security.title: The network edge as a defense-in-depth boundary
network-edge-security.subtitle: One request crosses from the hostile internet to your origin. It must survive four controls in order; each can deny and each writes an audit-log line. The abusive request (dashed) is rejected at the rate limiter before it ever reaches the app.

legend.label: untrusted zone + the abusive request
edge controls that enforce the boundary
trusted zone — the assets you protect
audit log — every deny is evidence

network-edge-security.title: The edge policy, one control at a time
network-edge-security.subtitle: The gateway/WAF config that enforces the boundary — default-deny, layered, and it writes an audit line on every reject.
network-edge-security.code:
# edge-policy.yaml — enforced at the API gateway (default DENY)
listen:
  tls:
    min_version: "1.3"          # confidentiality in transit; TLS 1.2 min floor
    hsts: "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload"

waf:
  ruleset: owasp-crs-4.0         # OWASP Core Rule Set: SQLi, XSS, path traversal
  mode: blocking                 # NOT detection-only — it must reject, not just log

rate_limit:
  per_ip:    { requests: 100, window: 60s, on_exceed: deny_429 }
  per_token: { requests: 600, window: 60s, on_exceed: deny_429 }

routes:
  default: deny                  # least privilege for traffic: allowlist, not blocklist
  allow:
    - path: /api/v1/orders
      methods: [GET, POST]
      auth: required            # authn happens at the edge, before the origin

audit:
  on_deny: log                  # every 403/429/WAF-block emits a structured line
  fields: [ts, src_ip, token_sub, path, control, decision]

steps.label: TLS — confidentiality only
steps.note: TLS 1.3 and HSTS stop eavesdropping and downgrade. Necessary, but this control alone protects nothing about who or what is inside the request.

steps.label: WAF in blocking mode
steps.note: The OWASP Core Rule Set inspects the decrypted payload for injection/XSS/traversal. The tell of a real control: mode is 'blocking', not 'detection-only'. Logging an attack you let through is not a defense.

steps.label: Rate limit per-IP AND per-token
steps.note: Volumetric abuse and credential stuffing are traffic-shape attacks. Per-IP catches the flood; per-token catches the authenticated scraper walking object IDs. on_exceed: deny_429 — it rejects, it does not queue.

steps.label: Default-deny routing
steps.note: Least privilege for traffic: the boundary allows the known-good and denies everything else. An allowlist fails closed; a blocklist forgets a path and fails open.

steps.label: Auth at the edge
steps.note: The gateway authenticates before the origin sees the request. The origin still re-checks authorization — the edge is the first gate, never the only one (defense in depth).

steps.label: Audit every deny
steps.note: This line turns a control into evidence. A structured record of (src_ip, token, path, which control, decision) is the exact artifact a reviewer inspects to confirm an abuse was actually rejected.

network-edge-security.caption: Fire the abuse at it: 150 requests/min from one IP → the rate limiter returns 429 and writes control=rate_limit, decision=deny to the audit log. The origin never sees request 101.

network-edge-security.text: OWASP Top 10 and the API Top 10 both map cleanly onto edge controls — A05 Security Misconfiguration and API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption are edge failures by construction. But the senior tell is that the edge is defense-in-depth, never the whole defense: authorization is still re-checked at the origin. An engineer who says 'the WAF handles it' has one boundary; an engineer who treats the edge as the first of several has a threat model.

network-edge-security.question: A reviewer challenge: your packet says 'the edge blocks SQL injection via the WAF.' What is the one piece of evidence that proves this is not just a happy-path claim?
options: A screenshot showing the WAF product is installed and licensed.
A captured request carrying a SQLi payload that returns a 403 from the WAF, plus the matching audit-log line naming the rule that fired — with the WAF in blocking, not detection-only, mode.
A paragraph in the packet explaining what SQL injection is.
A note that the application code uses parameterized queries.
network-edge-security.explanation: Proof is a denied abuse request plus its audit trail. Option 1 shows presence, not enforcement — a detection-only WAF is 'installed' and blocks nothing. Option 3 is understanding, not evidence. Option 4 is a real defense but it is the origin's control, not the edge's — it does not prove the edge blocks anything. Only option 2 shows the abuse hitting the boundary and being rejected there, with the log line a reviewer can inspect.

network-edge-security.intro: Prove your edge section holds — no vibes:
items: You named the assets behind the edge (what the boundary protects) — 'the whole app' is not an asset list; name the data and the actions.
The trust boundary is explicit: which zone is untrusted, which is trusted, and the exact line the request crosses.
Each control is present AND enforcing: your WAF is in blocking mode and your route policy is default-deny, not detection-only or default-allow.
You fired one concrete abuse case (flood, ID-enumeration, or injection) and captured the deny response — the status code AND which control rejected it.
The denial appears in an audit log with enough fields (src, token, path, control, decision) that a reviewer can reconstruct what happened without you narrating.

prompts: In your own words: why does 'behind HTTPS' protect confidentiality but leave the attack surface almost untouched?
Explain why the edge is default-deny (allowlist) rather than default-allow (blocklist), using your own route policy as the example.

Walk the abuse request through your edge out loud — which control denies it, and what does the audit-log line say? Then explain why the origin still re-checks authorization even though the edge already authenticated.

network-edge-security.subtitle: Both mention a WAF. Only one is a reviewable control that denies abuse.

left.label: Perimeter theater
lines: "App is behind HTTPS and a WAF"
WAF in detection-only mode (logs, never blocks)
Routes default-allow; new endpoints exposed silently
No rate limit — one IP can walk every object ID
No abuse case run; no deny captured; no audit line

right.label: Enforced edge (gold)

WAF blocking mode, OWASP CRS; route policy default-deny
Per-IP + per-token rate limits, on_exceed: deny_429
Abuse case fired: 150 req/min → 429 at the rate limiter
Audit log shows control=rate_limit, decision=deny

network-edge-security.caption: The difference is not the tools listed, it is whether a specific abusive request returns a deny you can point to in a log. Presence is not enforcement.

network-edge-security.text: The pattern is trust-boundary-with-enforced-controls, and it travels off the network entirely: a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is default-deny east-west traffic (same allowlist logic, pod-to-pod instead of internet-to-origin); a cloud security group is an edge control on a VPC subnet; even a mailroom that x-rays packages before they enter the building is a WAF for the physical edge. What stays invariant: name the boundary, default-deny, layer the controls, prove one abuse is rejected, log the denial. What changes with context: at higher scale you push rate limits to a CDN edge; under stricter compliance you add mTLS so even authenticated traffic proves its identity cryptographically. This same threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md carries into the security capstone — the edge section you just wrote becomes the outermost boundary of the full threat model, and its captured deny becomes one row in the exploit-regression suite. Next you take the request that survived the edge and decide what it is allowed to do inside the trusted zone: authorization.

data-protection-privacy.outcome: Take one real endpoint that returns user data and produce Section D of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: classify the PII it exposes, name the trust boundary it crosses, pick the data-protection control (field-level authz + minimization), and record the audit-log line that would prove an abuse attempt was denied.
data-protection-privacy.proof: Section D of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: a data-classification row (what PII, what sensitivity), the named trust boundary, the chosen control with its rejected alternative, one FAILING unauthorized request captured verbatim (status + body), and the matching audit-log entry. A reviewer can point to the denied request and the log line without you narrating.
data-protection-privacy.unlock: Your packet names the PII, marks the trust boundary, enforces least privilege at the field level, and shows a real denied request plus its audit-log evidence.
data-protection-privacy.doNotClaim: Do not claim data is protected because the route sits behind a login. Authentication answers who; data protection answers what this identity may see of THIS record. A packet with no denied-request transcript and no audit line is a description, not a control — it caps at 78.

data-protection-privacy.text: A support agent opens a ticket, the API returns the customer object, and buried in that JSON is the full SSN and a raw session token — because the endpoint was written to serve the owner and nobody re-checked it when support got read access. One over-broad response is now a breach-notification letter.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase of Security & Identity Engineering: you already frame threats, set trust boundaries, and enforce access control. Data protection is where those meet the payload — proving that a request which passes authentication still cannot exfiltrate PII it has no business seeing.

data-protection-privacy.prompt: GET /api/users/42 requires a valid session, and the code checks the caller is logged in. Is the data protected? Answer before reading on.
data-protection-privacy.reveal: No — that is authentication, not data protection. OWASP API Top 10 calls the gap here BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization, API1) plus Excessive Data Exposure (API3): a logged-in caller requests user 42's record and the server hands it over without asking whether THIS identity may read THAT object, or filtering which fields it may see. 'Logged in' is a doorway; the record is a vault. Protection is per-object, per-field, and it is the check almost everyone forgets because the happy path looks identical.

data-protection-privacy.title: Data protection = classify the PII, enforce least privilege per object and field, and prove denial
data-protection-privacy.text: Auth proves who you are. Data protection proves this identity may read THIS record, minimized to the fields it needs, with every denied attempt in the audit log. The invariant: no PII leaves without an object-level and field-level authorization check that can return 'no'.

data-protection-privacy.title: The data-protection path — failure vs repair
data-protection-privacy.subtitle: A request crosses the trust boundary into the user store. The failure path (top) authenticates then serves the full record. The repair path (bottom) adds object-level authz, field minimization, and an audit line on denial.

nodes.label: Object AuthZ
nodes.description: may THIS id read THIS record?

legend.label: failure path — authn-only, full record leaks
repair path — object authz + field minimization
denial proven in the audit log

data-protection-privacy.title: Section D of the packet — the enforced handler + its proof
data-protection-privacy.subtitle: Object-level authorization, field minimization, and the audit line — the artifact reviewers inspect.
data-protection-privacy.code:
# Section D — Data Protection: GET /api/users/{id}
# Classification: email(internal) name(internal) ssn(RESTRICTED) session_token(SECRET)
# Trust boundary: internet -> gateway -> user store. Selected: object authz + field minimization.

ALLOWED_FIELDS = {"self": {"email", "name", "ssn"}, "support": {"email", "name"}}

def get_user(caller, target_id):
    record = store.load(target_id)                       # PII in memory
    if not can_read_object(caller, record):              # OBJECT-level least privilege
        audit.log("access.denied", actor=caller.id, target=target_id,
                  reason="bola", scope=caller.role)       # denial is evidence
        raise Forbidden(403)
    scope = "self" if caller.id == record.id else caller.role
    fields = ALLOWED_FIELDS[scope]                        # MINIMIZE per identity
    return {k: record[k] for k in fields}                # ssn/token never leave for support

# PROOF (captured transcript):
#   support agent -> GET /api/users/42  => 403 Forbidden  (cross-tenant target)
#   audit: {"evt":"access.denied","actor":"agent_9","target":42,"reason":"bola"}
#   owner -> GET /api/users/42 => 200, body has NO ssn/session_token field

steps.label: Classify before you protect
steps.note: You cannot minimize what you have not labeled. ssn is RESTRICTED, session_token is SECRET — these must never appear in a support-scoped response. This row is the threat-model input.

steps.label: Least privilege as data, not code
steps.note: ALLOWED_FIELDS makes the field-level policy explicit and reviewable. 'support' can never see ssn because the set does not contain it — no code path can leak it.

steps.label: Object-level authz (the BOLA fix)
steps.note: The check that OWASP API1 exists to force: may THIS caller read THIS record? A test that can return 'no' — the deny raises 403 and writes the audit line before anything is returned.

steps.label: The denial IS the evidence
steps.note: audit.log on the deny path is what a reviewer inspects. No log entry means you cannot prove the abuse attempt was stopped — that gap caps the lesson at 78.

steps.label: Minimize on the allow path
steps.note: Even an authorized read returns only the fields that scope needs. Excessive Data Exposure (API3) is closed by construction: ssn and token are absent from support responses.

steps.label: Prove it — the failing request
steps.note: The captured 403 transcript plus the audit line plus the minimized 200 body are the proof. Without the denied request recorded verbatim, the packet is a claim, not a control.

data-protection-privacy.caption: A reviewer runs the cross-tenant request, sees the 403, finds the matching audit line, and confirms the owner's 200 body carries no ssn or token.

data-protection-privacy.subtitle: Both pass authentication. Only one protects the data.

No object-level check: any logged-in id reads any record (BOLA)

No field classification, no minimization

'It's behind auth' presented as the control
left.verdict: Excessive exposure + BOLA — caps at 78, no proof of denial

can_read_object() can return 'no' → 403 (least privilege per object)

data-protection-privacy.caption: The tell: the gold handler's authorization check can say 'no', and there is a recorded request where it did. A control you cannot watch deny is decoration.

data-protection-privacy.text: OWASP API Top 10 ranks Broken Object Level Authorization (API1) as the #1 API risk precisely because it hides behind working authentication — the happy path is byte-identical to the exploit. Data protection lives one layer past the login: classify the PII, authorize the object, minimize the fields, and log the denial. If your evidence is 'it requires a token,' you have described authentication and named it protection.

data-protection-privacy.question: Reviewer challenge: which single piece of evidence best proves the endpoint is protected against Broken Object Level Authorization, not just understood?
options: A sentence in the packet stating that the route requires a valid session.
A captured transcript of an authenticated cross-tenant request returning 403, plus the matching audit-log 'access.denied' entry.
A screenshot showing the owner successfully retrieving their own record with a 200.
A comment in the code that says '# TODO: add object-level authorization check'.
data-protection-privacy.explanation: BOLA is about a valid session reading someone else's object. Only option 2 shows the authorization check actually returning 'no' for a cross-tenant caller AND leaving audit evidence of the denial — the falsifiable proof. A session requirement (1) is authentication; a happy-path 200 (3) never exercises the deny branch; a TODO (4) is the vulnerability, not the control.

data-protection-privacy.intro: Prove Section D holds — no vibes:
items: Every field returned is classified (public / internal / restricted / secret). If ssn or session_token appears in any response scope, name why it is allowed or remove it.
The object-level check can return 'no': write the exact request (caller + target) that must produce a 403, then run it and capture the response verbatim.
The denied request has a matching audit-log line with actor, target, and reason. No log entry = you cannot prove denial = the lesson caps at 78.
The authorized (owner) response is inspected and confirmed free of restricted/secret fields — minimization actually happened, not just intended.
Least privilege is data, not scattered ifs: a reviewer can read one policy table (ALLOWED_FIELDS) and predict every response without reading the handler.

prompts: Explain, using your own endpoint, why authentication passing does NOT mean the data is protected — and name the OWASP risk that gap maps to.
Walk the failure path and the repair path of your diagram out loud: where exactly does the full record leak, and which check stops it?

Point a skeptical reviewer to the single line of evidence that proves your object-level authorization can deny — the denied request and its audit entry — and explain why a happy-path 200 would not satisfy them.

data-protection-privacy.text: The pattern is invariant across every asset that carries PII: classify, authorize per object, minimize per field, log the denial. What changes is the boundary. A multi-tenant SaaS row swaps 'is this my record' for 'is this my tenant' (the same BOLA check, wider blast radius). A GDPR export endpoint adds a purpose-limitation field to the classification. A logs pipeline moves the minimizer upstream so secrets never reach the sink. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the security capstone unchanged in structure — its denied-request transcript and audit line become the exploit-regression test the capstone reuses. If the packet cannot be reused there, it was never premium-ready.

logging-detection-response.outcome: Take one real authorization boundary (e.g. "admin deletes another tenant's object") and build the detection slice of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: the audit event you emit on that action, one falsifiable detection rule over it, and the response runbook the alert fires. Not a note — a reviewable artifact with the failing unauthorized request, the audit-log evidence, and the alert it should raise.
logging-detection-response.proof: The detection section of threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: a structured audit event (who/what/resource/decision/outcome), one detection rule that fires on the abuse case and stays silent on normal traffic, and a runbook link. Proof = the unauthorized request logged, the rule matching it, and a tuning note showing the false-positive rate you accept. A reviewer replays the abuse case and sees the alert fire.
logging-detection-response.unlock: Your slice emits a structured audit event on the boundary crossing, a detection rule that fires on abuse and is silent on baseline, and a response runbook the alert triggers.
logging-detection-response.doNotClaim: Do not claim "we have logging" if you log the happy path but not the DENIED decision, or if the log has no detection rule over it. A log nobody queries and an alert nobody routes to a runbook is detection theater — you have a data lake, not a control.

logging-detection-response.text: The breach report lands: the attacker had valid credentials and moved for eleven days. Every action was in the logs the whole time. Nobody was watching the one line that said access_decision=DENY, retried 400 times.

Logging, detection, and response is the synthesis layer of this course: it turns the identity, least-privilege, and threat-model work from earlier lessons into evidence a reviewer can replay. Without it, a control that "prevents" abuse has no proof it ever fired — and no way to catch the abuse it missed.

logging-detection-response.prompt: An attacker with a stolen token hits your API. Which single log line is the highest-signal detection — the successful reads they made, or something else? Decide before reading.
logging-detection-response.reveal: Neither the reads nor the errors — it's the DENIED authorization decisions. Successful reads look identical to legitimate traffic; 500s are noise. But a burst of access_decision=DENY from one identity across many resources is an attacker probing the boundary, and it is nearly invisible in normal traffic. The highest-signal event is the control saying "no" — most teams log the "yes" and drop the "no".

logging-detection-response.title: Detect-respond is one loop: emit the decision, alert on abuse, route to a runbook
logging-detection-response.text: Log the authorization DECISION (allow and deny) as a structured audit event, write a detection rule that fires on the abuse case yet stays silent on baseline, and wire the alert to a runbook. The invariant: every control emits evidence, and every high-signal event has an owner who acts.

logging-detection-response.title: The detect-respond pipeline — and where it silently breaks
logging-detection-response.subtitle: An action crosses an authorization boundary → audit event → collector → detection rule → alert → triage → incident + runbook. The failure path (no deny logged, or an alert with no owner) is marked; the repair is the DENY event feeding a tuned rule.

logging-detection-response.title: The detection slice, one block at a time
logging-detection-response.subtitle: A structured audit event plus a Sigma-style rule over it — the exact artifact from Build, filled.
logging-detection-response.code:
## Detection slice — cross-tenant object access
# 1) Structured audit event emitted at the authz control point
{ "ts":"2026-07-01T14:22:07Z", "actor":"user:admin-42", "actor_tenant":"acme",
  "action":"object.delete", "resource":"obj:9f21", "resource_tenant":"globex",
  "access_decision":"DENY", "reason":"cross_tenant", "src_ip":"10.2.9.7", "request_id":"r-8831" }

# 2) Detection rule (Sigma) — fires on repeated cross-tenant DENY from one actor
detection:
  selection:
    access_decision: DENY
    reason: cross_tenant
  timeframe: 10m
  condition: selection | count() by actor > 5   # baseline: legit users ~0/10m
level: high

# 3) Response — the runbook this alert triggers
response: runbooks/cross-tenant-access.md   # suspend token -> confirm scope -> open incident

steps.label: Log the DECISION, not just the request
steps.note: access_decision:DENY with reason:cross_tenant is the high-signal field. actor_tenant vs resource_tenant is the boundary — logging both is what makes the abuse detectable.

steps.label: The rule must be able to stay silent
steps.note: selection matches ONLY cross-tenant denies. A rule that also fires on normal 403s is noise; least privilege at the query layer too.

steps.label: A threshold tuned against baseline
steps.note: >5 in 10m separates a fat-finger from probing. State the baseline (legit ~0) so the false-positive cost is explicit — that tuning note IS the proof it is not theater.

steps.label: Alert routes to a runbook, not an inbox
steps.note: level:high plus a named runbook means the alert has an owner and a first action (suspend token). An alert with no runbook is a log line with anxiety.

logging-detection-response.caption: Replay the abuse case: fire 6 cross-tenant deletes, watch the rule match, confirm the runbook opens. That transcript is the reviewable evidence.

logging-detection-response.caption: The difference is not volume of logs — it's logging the DENY decision, putting a falsifiable rule over it, and giving the alert an owner.

logging-detection-response.text: Grounded in the NICE Framework and OWASP: the OWASP Top 10 lists "Security Logging and Monitoring Failures" as a category precisely because most teams log the happy path and never detect the abuse. The senior tell — you log the DENIED decision and can prove, with a replay, that your rule fires on abuse and stays silent on baseline. Detection you can't demonstrate firing is a hope, not a control.

logging-detection-response.question: A reviewer says: "Point to the exact evidence this detection works, not just that you understand it." What must you show?
options: A screenshot of your log volume dashboard proving lots of data is collected.
The failing unauthorized request in the audit log, the rule matching it, the alert firing, AND a tuning note showing it stays silent on baseline — replayable.
A written description of the threat model and why cross-tenant access is bad.
A high count of total alerts fired last month, proving the system is active.
logging-detection-response.explanation: Proof of detection is a replay: the abuse case (the DENIED cross-tenant request) present in the audit log, the rule matching that exact event, the alert firing, and evidence it does NOT fire on normal traffic (the tuning/false-positive note). Log volume (1), prose (3), and raw alert counts (4) show activity, not that this control catches this abuse — a noisy rule with a high count can be pure false positives.

logging-detection-response.intro: Prove the detection slice is real — no vibes:
items: Your audit event logs the access_decision for BOTH allow and deny, with actor, action, resource, and reason as structured fields — not a free-text line.
You replayed the abuse case (the unauthorized cross-tenant request) and confirmed it appears in the audit log with decision=DENY.
Your detection rule fired on that replay AND you checked it stays silent on a sample of normal traffic — record the baseline false-positive rate you accept.
The alert routes to a named owner and a runbook whose first action is concrete (suspend token / confirm scope / open incident), not "investigate".
You logged a repair note: one way the rule could miss (evasion below threshold, or a boundary that emits no deny) and the tuning change that closes it.

prompts: Explain why the DENIED authorization decision is higher-signal for detection than the successful requests — using your own boundary as the example.
Walk through your detection slice: the audit event, the rule, and the runbook — and say what makes the rule falsifiable (able to stay silent).
Which part of your slice is weakest — the log, the rule threshold, or the response owner — and what is the reusable repair, not "watch more closely"?

logging-detection-response.text: The same loop — emit the decision, detect the abuse, route to a runbook — transfers to any boundary in the security capstone: a secret read outside its allowed service, an IAM role assumed from a new region, an API rate limit tripped by one key. What stays invariant is logging the DENY and putting a tuned, falsifiable rule over it with an owner. What changes with scale is the tuning: at low volume you alert on a single deny; at high volume you need a threshold and a baseline or you drown in false positives. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the capstone — its detection slice plus the replayed abuse case is the evidence that your threat model is enforced, not just described.

A reviewer can replay the denial from your evidence without you narrating.
incident-response.unlock: Your packet shows a real asset, a trust boundary, a least-privilege control, a denied unauthorized request, and the audit-log line that proves the denial was observed — not just described.
incident-response.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'we do incident response' because you wrote a runbook prose paragraph. A runbook with no captured denial and no audit-log evidence is a happy-path answer. The invariant: the control's refusal must be OBSERVED (logged), not merely asserted.

The question is not 'how do we patch it' — it is 'what evidence proves this account was ever allowed to, and where is the log line that should have screamed no?' Incident Response is the discipline that has that answer before the bridge asks.

This lesson sits in the synthesis phase of Security & Identity Engineering — it fuses identity, least-privilege authorization, audit logging, and detection into one reviewable act. Incident Response is where a threat model stops being a diagram and becomes evidence that a control actually denied an abuse and logged it.

incident-response.reveal: The observed denial. A check that returns 403 but writes nothing to the audit log is invisible during an incident — you cannot prove it fired, cannot alert on it, and cannot reconstruct who tried. Incident readiness is not 'the control exists'; it is 'the control's refusal is captured as evidence.' The invariant of this lesson: a denial you cannot find in the audit log did not happen, as far as the responder is concerned.

incident-response.intro: Prove your packet is incident-ready — every item must be inspectable, not asserted:
items: The asset and the trust boundary it lives behind are named explicitly (which request, crossing which edge, touching which store).
The access matrix is written: for each role, exactly which actions on the asset are granted — support must NOT include the privileged action.
One abuse case exists as a real (or replayable) unauthorized request, and it was DENIED — you have the 403, not a description of a 403.
The audit log has a captured DENY line with actor, action, and reason (least-privilege-violation) — the denial is OBSERVED, so detection can alert on it.
The repair retest passes: the legitimate privileged role still succeeds, proving the control is least-privilege, not a blanket wall.
The packet records context, assumptions, selected vs rejected approach, expected failure, reviewer objection, and the capstone connection.

Point it at a multi-tenant boundary: the asset becomes tenant B's data, the abuse case becomes tenant A's token requesting GET /tenants/B/records, the control becomes tenant-scoping, and the observed denial becomes a cross-tenant DENY audit line detection alerts on. What stays invariant: name the asset, deny the abuse case, and PROVE the denial was observed. What changes with scale, risk, and privacy: cross-tenant leakage is often silent-allow (data returned, nothing logged) — so the audit evidence matters even more, and a compliance constraint (data-residency, GDPR) may raise the bar from 'log the denial' to 'log every access decision, allow and deny.'

compliance-evidence.outcome: Take one authorization boundary you own (or a realistic one) and produce threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md: the asset, the access matrix, one abuse case, a FAILING unauthorized request, the audit-log line that recorded the denial, and a repair retest. Compliance evidence is not a claim that a control exists — it is the artifact that PROVES it fired.

An auditor reads it and can reproduce the denial without you narrating.
compliance-evidence.unlock: Your packet shows a real denied request AND the audit log that recorded the denial — evidence a reviewer can replay, not prose asserting the control works.
compliance-evidence.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'the control is compliant' from a passing happy-path test. A 200 for an authorized user proves nothing about the boundary. Evidence is the DENIAL that fired plus the log that captured it. A screenshot with no reproducible request, or a control with no audit trail, is a claim wearing evidence's clothes.

compliance-evidence.text: The auditor asks one question — 'Show me the exact moment this control stopped an attacker' — and the room that has been saying 'yes, we enforce least privilege' for a year goes silent, because a policy in a doc is not evidence, and nobody kept the log.

Every control you have built across this course — identity, sessions, authorization, object access, secrets, IAM — is worthless to a reviewer until you can prove it FIRED on a real abuse attempt. Compliance evidence is the synthesis lesson: it packages a denied request plus its audit trail into an artifact the capstone and an external auditor can both replay.

compliance-evidence.prompt: You wrote an authorization check and a unit test that confirms an admin can delete a record (returns 200). Is that evidence the access control is compliant? Answer before reading on.
compliance-evidence.reveal: No — it is the opposite of evidence. A passing test for the ALLOWED path only proves the door opens for people who have the key; it says nothing about whether it stays SHUT for everyone else. Compliance evidence is the DENIED case: a non-owner hits the endpoint, gets a 403, and the audit log records 'user 42 DENIED delete on record 7 at 14:02'. The evidence is the refusal plus the receipt for the refusal — an auditor can replay both. A green happy-path test is a control's alibi, not its proof.

compliance-evidence.title: Evidence = a denied abuse case + the audit log that recorded the denial
compliance-evidence.text: The invariant: a control is only proven by a reproducible refusal plus its audit trail. Package the asset, the access matrix, one abuse case, the failing unauthorized request, and the matching log line. No denial and no log means no evidence — only a claim.

## Context
- Asset: order records; least-privilege invariant = owner-only delete
## Access matrix (role x action x resource)
- owner   | delete | own record    -> ALLOW
- member  | delete | others record -> DENY   (abuse case)

- user 42 (member) attempts: DELETE /records/7  (record 7 owned by user 9)

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer u42' \

403
## Audit-log evidence (append-only)
{"ts":"2026-07-01T14:02:11Z","actor":42,"action":"delete",

## Reviewer objection & repair retest

steps.note: State the least-privilege rule in one line: owner-only delete. Vague scope means unfalsifiable evidence.

steps.label: The abuse case (map to OWASP)

steps.label: The FAILING request

steps.label: The audit-log line

compliance-evidence.text: The standard the auditor is actually holding: OWASP API Top 10 (API1 Broken Object Level Authorization) and the NICE Framework both demand that a control be VERIFIABLE, not merely declared. Mapping your abuse case to a named standard turns 'we check ownership' into 'we deny API1 and here is the logged proof' — that mapping is what separates a control from evidence of a control.

compliance-evidence.question: A reviewer says: 'Point me to the exact evidence that this is not just a happy-path answer.' Which response is real compliance evidence?
options: A unit test showing the resource owner successfully deletes their own record (200 OK).
A replayable unauthorized request that returns 403, the matching append-only audit-log line recording actor/action/decision=DENY, and a check that the row was untouched.
A policy document stating that only owners may delete records.
A screenshot of the authorization code with the ownership check highlighted.
compliance-evidence.explanation: Only option 2 is evidence a reviewer can REPLAY: the denial fired (403), it was recorded (audit line with decision=DENY), and the abuse had no side effect (row untouched). The happy-path 200 (1) proves the door opens, not that it stays shut. A policy (3) and highlighted code (4) are claims that the control SHOULD exist — neither proves it FIRED on the abuse case.

compliance-evidence.intro: Prove your evidence packet is real — no vibes:
items: The abuse case is a genuine unauthorized action (a non-owner / wrong role), mapped to a named standard (e.g. OWASP API1), not a happy-path request.
The unauthorized request is REPLAYABLE and returns a denial (403/401). If it only exists as prose or a screenshot, capture the actual request/response.
There is an audit-log line that records who, what, when, and decision=DENY — and it is append-only (an attacker cannot erase their own denial).
You confirmed no side effect: the target row/resource is untouched, proving the deny did not partially execute.
A repair retest exists: after the control is (re)applied, the same abuse request is re-run and still denied AND still logged.

# Threat Model + Access Control Packet — GET /invoices/{id}

## Context & assumptions
- Asset: customer invoices (financial PII). Multi-tenant; every invoice has owner_id.
- Assumption: authN works (valid JWT = a real subject). authZ is UNPROVEN — that is the target.
- Trust boundary: the object-access boundary — subject → specific invoice object.

## Access matrix (subject x object -> decision)
| subject        | invoice.owner = self | invoice.owner = other | admin scope |
| user (tenant A)| ALLOW read           | DENY (403 + audit)    | DENY        |
| admin          | ALLOW read           | ALLOW read (scoped)   | ALLOW       |

## Selected control (least privilege)
- Object-level authorization: deny by default; ALLOW iff invoice.owner_id == subject.id
  (or subject has admin scope). Enforced server-side, per request, on the object.

## Rejected control
- URL/role check only ("is a logged-in user"): authenticates but does not authorize
  the OBJECT -> classic BOLA / IDOR (OWASP API Top 10 #1). Rejected.

## Expected failure (abuse case)
- User A (owns 0001) requests GET /invoices/4172 (owned by tenant B).
- Expected: 403, no invoice body, one audit_log row {decision:deny, reason:owner_mismatch}.

## Verification method
- Failing unauthorized request test (below) + audit-log assertion. Deny is PROVEN, not claimed.

## Reviewer objection & repair
- Objection: "Your test only checks 403 status." Repair: also assert body is empty AND
  the audit row exists -> a 403 that still leaks the object in the error is not a deny.

## Capstone connection
- Reused in the security capstone: this packet + its exploit-regression test become the
  BOLA control in the threat model, IAM policy, and detection runbook.

steps.note: Subject × object × decision, deny-by-default. 'user requesting other's invoice → DENY' is the whole abuse case in one cell — an interviewer can read the policy at a glance.

steps.label: Selected control, enforced server-side per object
steps.note: owner_id == subject.id, checked on the object every request. Not a role flag, not a URL guard — the object itself is authorized.

steps.label: Name what you REJECTED and why
steps.note: A logged-in-only check is authentication masquerading as authorization → BOLA. Naming the rejected option and mapping it to OWASP API #1 is what separates gold from vocabulary.

steps.note: A requests 4172 (B's). Expected: 403, empty body, one audit row. Concrete ids make the failure reproducible — theatre can't survive a real id.

steps.label: Survive the objection
steps.note: A 403 that still echoes the object in its error message is a leak, not a deny. Assert status AND empty body AND audit row — this is the repair that makes it review-proof.

Objection-ready: asserts body empty AND audit row, not just 403
right.verdict: Denies the abuse case WITH proof — maps to OWASP API #1

security-interview-practice.caption: The gap is not knowledge of the words — it is whether a denied request and an audit-log line exist. Evidence beats vocabulary in every review.

security-interview-practice.text: Grounded in OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/API #1) is the most exploited API flaw precisely because auth checks the user, not the object. Interviewers reach for the invoice/order/document question because it separates candidates who authenticate from candidates who authorize. The NICE Framework calls this the Securely Provision + Protect-and-Defend seam — say it in the object's terms, not the user's.

security-interview-practice.question: Reviewer challenge: "Point to the exact evidence that this is not just a happy-path answer." Which response actually satisfies it?
options: "I explained least privilege and named the OWASP category, so the concept is covered."
"Here is the failing request — A requests B's invoice id 4172 → 403 with an empty body — and the matching audit_log row {decision:deny, reason:owner_mismatch}."
"My access matrix shows user-requesting-other → DENY, which proves the design is correct."
"The test returns 403, which is the standard deny status code."
security-interview-practice.explanation: The reviewer challenge demands the artifact, the broken case, and the proof output — not a design or a status code. Only option 2 points to a real denied request AND the audit-log evidence that the deny fired. The matrix (3) is design intent, not proof; a bare 403 (4) can still leak the object in its error body; naming the concept (1) is the vocabulary trap the challenge exists to catch.

security-interview-practice.intro: Prove your interview answer is an artifact, not a claim — no vibes:
items: Your packet names ONE asset and the ONE trust boundary it crosses (object-access, not just 'the API'). If it's generic, it's not a threat model.
The access matrix has a deny-by-default cell for 'subject requesting an object it does not own' — the abuse case is visible in the policy, not just in prose.
There is a failing UNAUTHORIZED request: subject A, object owned by B, expected 403. If your test only proves the allow path, you proved nothing about denial.
The deny is asserted three ways: status 403, empty body (no object leak in the error), AND one audit_log row recording the denial.
You named the REJECTED control (logged-in-only / URL check) and mapped it to BOLA / OWASP API #1 — a reviewer can see what you chose against and why.
You can answer the objection 'your 403 still leaks the object' with the repair already in the packet — closed-note.

prompts: Problem → context → artifact: state the interview question, why authentication doesn't answer it, and which artifact you hand over — in your own words.
Failure → proof: describe the abuse case (who requests whose object) and the exact evidence — the failing request plus the audit-log line — that proves the deny fired.
Tradeoff → repair: name the control you rejected, why it maps to BOLA, and the one repair that survives the reviewer's 'your 403 still leaks the object' objection.

security-interview-practice.text: The pattern is invariant across every security interview prompt; only the asset and attacker path change. "Stop a user from editing another team's document" (object access → same matrix, same audit proof). "A leaked API token — contain the blast radius" (secret + least-privilege scope + audit trail). "Prove your admin action was authorized" (identity + role scope + evidence). What stays fixed: name the asset, draw the boundary, write the least-privilege rule as a matrix, deny an abuse case, and point to audit evidence. What changes with user, tenant, risk, and compliance constraint is which object, which scope, and which log. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the capstone unchanged in structure — it becomes the BOLA control in your threat model, exploit-regression test, IAM policy, and detection runbook. You no longer talk about security in interviews. You hand over proof.

security-capstone.outcome: Take one privileged user action that crosses an authorization boundary (e.g. "tenant admin exports another tenant's records") and assemble the whole course into one reviewable artifact: threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md — assets, trust boundaries, an access matrix, the least-privilege control, the abuse case it denies, a failing unauthorized request, audit-log evidence, and the incident runbook that fires when the control trips.
security-capstone.proof: threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger, containing: context + assumptions, assets + trust boundaries, an access matrix, the selected control, the rejected control, the abuse case, a captured 403 on the unauthorized request, the audit-log line proving denial, a reviewer objection with repair notes, and the capstone connection. A reviewer can replay the denial from the packet alone.
security-capstone.unlock: Your packet names assets and trust boundaries, enforces least privilege in a matrix, and PROVES a cross-boundary abuse case is denied with a real failing request plus its audit-log line.
security-capstone.doNotClaim: Do not claim the control works because the happy path passed. "My authorized request returned 200" proves nothing about abuse. The proof is the UNAUTHORIZED request returning 403 AND the audit log recording the denied attempt. A packet with no failing request and no audit line is a description, not evidence.

security-capstone.text: A tenant admin clicks Export, and the API hands back another company's customer list — no error, no alarm, no log. That is a real breach (OWASP API1: Broken Object Level Authorization), and tonight you assemble every skill in this course into the one packet that proves it can't happen.

You have spent this course learning identity, sessions, authorization, object access, secrets, API security, threat modeling, attack trees, cloud IAM, detection, and incidents as separate skills. The capstone fuses them: one boundary, one control, one denied abuse case, one audit trail — a single artifact a reviewer can inspect and replay.

security-capstone.prompt: Your authorization test suite is green: every allowed user gets a 200. Ship it? Decide before reading on.
security-capstone.reveal: No — green happy-path tests are the classic BOLA blind spot. Authorization is proven by what it DENIES, not what it allows. The test that matters is user A requesting user B's object and getting 403 — plus an audit-log line recording the attempt. A suite that never fires an unauthorized request has never tested the boundary at all; it has confirmed the door opens, not that it locks.

security-capstone.title: A secure workflow is a proven denial across a trust boundary
security-capstone.text: Name the assets and the trust boundary they cross. Enforce least privilege at that boundary. Then PROVE it: a real cross-boundary request is denied (403) and the denial is logged. Invariant — no control counts until its abuse case fails and the failure is evidenced.

security-capstone.title: The assembled system: request to denied-and-logged
security-capstone.subtitle: Every prior skill is a node on one path — identity → session → authorization → object access → audit → detection → incident. The abuse case (Tenant A reaching Tenant B's object) hits the authz boundary, is denied, and the denial fires detection.

legend.label: the trust boundary + its denial path
identity in, audit out
least-privilege allow (own tenant only)

security-capstone.title: The control + its proof, in one slice
security-capstone.subtitle: An object-level authorization check that denies cross-tenant access AND logs it — the exact artifact the packet references.
security-capstone.code:
def authorize_export(session, record_id, audit):
    record = records.get(record_id)          # object under access
    subject_tenant = session.tenant_id        # from verified identity
    owner_tenant = record.tenant_id           # object's real owner

    allowed = subject_tenant == owner_tenant  # least-privilege: own tenant only

    audit.write(                              # log EVERY decision, allow or deny
        actor=session.user_id,
        action="export",
        object=record_id,
        decision="allow" if allowed else "deny",
        reason="cross_tenant_bola" if not allowed else None,
    )
    if not allowed:
        raise Forbidden(403)               # deny the abuse case, do not leak data
    return record

steps.label: Object-level, not just role-level
steps.note: RBAC alone ("is admin") passes the abuse case. The invariant is comparing the SUBJECT's tenant to the OBJECT's owner — the OWASP API1 BOLA check that role checks miss.

steps.label: Least privilege as one boolean
steps.note: An admin of Tenant A has zero privilege over Tenant B's objects. The boundary is this line; everything else is enforcement and evidence.

steps.label: Audit before you branch
steps.note: Log the decision — allow AND deny — before raising. A deny with no audit line is invisible to detection; the log IS the proof, not a nicety.

steps.label: Fail closed
steps.note: 403, not a filtered 200 that silently drops rows. Fail-closed + a reason code (cross_tenant_bola) is what detection keys on.

security-capstone.caption: The passing proof is the UNAUTHORIZED call: authorize_export(tenant_A_session, tenant_B_record) raises 403 and writes decision="deny" — replayable from the packet.

security-capstone.text: OWASP puts Broken Object Level Authorization at API1 because it is the most common and most damaging API flaw — and it hides behind green tests. The NICE Framework frames this as the securely-provision + protect-and-defend loop: you don't just build the control, you produce the audit evidence that a defender and an auditor can both replay.

security-capstone.question: A reviewer asks: "Show me the exact evidence this packet works in the capstone, not just in theory." Which response actually proves it?
options: The threat model lists BOLA as a risk and the code has an authorization function.
A captured request where Tenant A asks for Tenant B's record and receives 403, plus the matching audit-log line with decision="deny", reason=cross_tenant_bola.
All authorized users successfully exported their own records (200 across the board).
The access matrix shows admins have export permission and the RBAC roles are documented.
The team agreed in review that the design looks secure.
security-capstone.explanation: Only option 2 is evidence of DENIAL across the boundary: a real failing unauthorized request AND its audit line. The threat model (1) and matrix (4) are design, not proof; the happy-path 200s (3) are the exact BOLA blind spot; consensus (5) is opinion. The reviewer challenge is met only by a replayable denied request with its log.

security-capstone.subtitle: Same threat (cross-tenant export). One describes security; one demonstrates it.

security-capstone.caption: The difference is a single failing request and its audit line. Everything left of it is a description; everything right of it is proof.

items: The abuse case is written as a concrete cross-boundary action (Tenant A → Tenant B's object), not "unauthorized access" in the abstract.
You ran the UNAUTHORIZED request and captured a real 403 (or equivalent deny) — not just asserted it would fail.
The audit log shows the denied attempt with actor, object, decision=deny, and a reason code — findable in the log, not just claimed.
The access matrix has at least one DENY cell, and that cell is the one you exercised.
A rejected control is named (e.g. RBAC-only) with WHY it fails the abuse case — role check passes BOLA.
The incident runbook states what fires when detection sees repeated denials, and one repair retest is recorded after a reviewer objection.

prompts: Roll-call the course: name each skill on the diagram (identity, session, authorization, object access, audit, detection, incident) and what it contributes to denying this one abuse case.
Explain why an RBAC role check passes the BOLA abuse case, and what the object-level check adds — using your own access matrix.
Point to the single line of evidence that would convince a skeptical auditor this is not a happy-path answer, and say why the audit log matters as much as the 403.

security-capstone.text: You arrived able to name security concepts; you leave able to assemble them into one artifact that PROVES a boundary holds — and that is the whole job. The same packet pattern travels to any boundary: a new asset (payment tokens), a new attacker path (privilege escalation via IAM role assumption), a new tenant boundary (region-isolated data under GDPR), a new abuse case (mass export). What stays invariant is the shape — assets, boundary, least-privilege control, a denied abuse case, audit evidence, runbook. What changes is the object, the blast radius, and the compliance constraint. Carry threat_model_and_access_control_packet.md into the capstone unchanged in structure: it is not "I understand security" — it is "here is a boundary I threat-modeled, controlled, attacked, denied, logged, and can replay for you right now."
